skills.name: Scandinavian modern tableware
skills.thesis: A few plain shapes that stack, a warm satin glaze and a quiet hand mark make tableware that is made in a factory but feels human.
skills.summary: Plain, stackable tableware from the factories of Finland and Sweden. Artists on the staff of the factory design simple forms in a few shapes, glaze them in satin or matt colours, and add a quiet hand mark.
use_cases: a calm Nordic kitchen or table scene
a museum label on 1950s Finnish and Swedish ceramics

skills.name: Abstract Expressionist ceramics
skills.thesis: The pot is a place for a gesture: a thrown cylinder can be cut, torn and stacked like paint on a canvas, and the use of the vessel no longer sets the form.
skills.summary: American ceramics after 1954 in which the potter treats the vessel as a sculpture. Peter Voulkos threw large forms, cut, tore and stacked them, and painted them with the gesture of action painting.
use_cases: a large sculptural vessel for a gallery
a museum label on 1950s American ceramic sculpture

wall_thickness.note: Large forms have a wall of 10 to 25 mm so that they can stand.

skills.name: Glass-ceramic cookware
skills.thesis: A cook wants one pot that goes from the freezer to the flame to the table, so the body is a glass that heat turns into a fine crystal ceramic.
skills.summary: Oven and flame ware made of a white glass-ceramic, a glass that is crystallised by heat. The body takes the gas flame and the freezer, and a blue cornflower decal marks the early range.
use_cases: a retro kitchen set dressing of 1960
a museum label on early glass-ceramic ware
a cookware brief for a white, flameproof casserole

wall_thickness.note: A glass-ceramic wall is thin and even because the heat must spread.

skills.name: West German fat lava
skills.thesis: A thick glaze that is allowed to run, bubble and crater gives a mass-made vase the look of cooled volcanic rock.
skills.summary: Vases and bowls from West German factories between 1960 and 1980. A thick, bubbled and cratered glaze runs over a moulded earthenware body, in orange, brown, green or yellow.
use_cases: a 1970s interior prompt with a bold vase
a museum label on West German ceramics

skills.name: Funk ceramics
skills.thesis: Clay is a rude, funny material, so a sculptor can make a toilet, a typewriter or a bust of himself and treat high art as a joke.
skills.summary: Hand-built ceramic sculpture from California that turns toilets, typewriters, self-portraits and bad taste into loud, crude and funny figures. Bright low-fire glazes and drips keep the clay rude.
use_cases: a gallery label for funk sculpture
a prompt for a loud, funny ceramic figure
a brief for a studio ceramic with a joke

skills.name: Large-format porcelain tiles
skills.thesis: One large, dense, thin sheet of ceramic makes a seamless surface that holds the look of another material.
skills.summary: Very hard, dense tiles that a factory presses in sizes of 60 by 60 cm and above, up to slabs of 3 m. A digital printer gives the surface the look of stone, wood or concrete. Fine joints make the wall or floor read as one skin.
use_cases: a modern floor or wall with a stone or concrete look
a worktop or facade in thin ceramic
a minimal interior with few joints

skills.name: Washlet toilet
skills.thesis: A toilet is a clean machine for the body, so the ceramic stays smooth and the seat adds water, heat and control.
skills.summary: A vitreous china WC with a heated seat, a warm-water spray nozzle and a control panel. The ceramic is plain and smooth, and the technology lives in the seat and the cistern.
use_cases: a product brief for a smart toilet
a hotel bathroom render in the Japanese style
a spec for a seat with a warm-water nozzle

wall_thickness.note: A pressure-cast bowl keeps an even wall of 8 to 12 mm.

skills.name: Memphis postmodern ceramics
skills.thesis: A vase is a toy, a totem and a joke at the same time: its form is a stack of simple solids, and its surface is a pattern in loud colour.
skills.summary: Ceramic vessels from the Memphis group of Milan after 1981. They combine plain geometric solids with loud colour and patterns of stripes, dots and terrazzo, and they ignore good taste.
use_cases: a loud postmodern vase or jar
a museum label on Italian ceramics of 1982

skills.name: Terracotta rainscreen
skills.thesis: A wall of fired clay can be a light, ventilated skin: the panel keeps the rain from the insulation, and the air behind it dries the wall.
skills.summary: A modern wall skin of extruded, hollow terracotta panels that hang on rails with an air gap behind them. The clay face is matt, flat and in earth colours, with a thin glaze or an engobe.
use_cases: a render of a modern building with a clay facade
a detail drawing of a ventilated terracotta wall
a facade material brief with an earth colour

ornament_level.note: Ornament stays low; the grid, the depth and the shadow give the variety.

wall_thickness.note: The panel wall is 15 to 30 mm, with webs inside.

skills.name: Designer wall-hung sanitary ware
skills.thesis: A bathroom fitting is a designed object, so the ceramic has a clear, simple shape that floats off the floor.
skills.summary: Sanitary ware that a famous designer shapes as a clean object. A WC hangs on the wall, the cistern hides in the wall, and a basin sits on the counter as a thin, sharp bowl.
use_cases: a render of a minimal spa bathroom
a product spec for a design collection

wall_thickness.note: A fine vitreous basin keeps a wall of 6 mm.

skills.name: Chef studio tableware
skills.thesis: A chef and a potter design the plate with the dish: a matt, earthy and slightly uneven vessel gives the food a ground that no factory plate can give.
skills.summary: Hand-made stoneware plates and bowls that a studio potter makes with a chef for one restaurant. The pieces have an uneven rim, a matt or earth-toned glaze and a bare clay foot, and they frame the food like a landscape.

skills.name: Digital 3D-printed ceramics
skills.thesis: When a machine builds the form from a file, the vessel can have a shape that no wheel or mould can make, and the layer line becomes the ornament.
skills.summary: Vessels that a machine builds layer by layer from a clay paste, after a digital model. The visible layer lines, the open lattice and the complex curves give the style its look.
use_cases: a parametric vase or lamp shade for a modern interior
a museum label on digital ceramics

wall_thickness.note: Printed walls can be very thin, but a lattice needs a minimum of 1 mm.

skills.name: Medieval court cuisine
skills.thesis: Make the table show rank: use costly spices, bright colour and many dishes at once, and let each sauce mix sweet, sour and hot.
skills.summary: The kitchen of the late medieval court. Cooks grind spices, thicken sauces with bread and colour the dish with saffron. Sweet, sour and hot flavours meet in one sauce. Le Viandier, first written about 1300 and widened by Taillevent, records it.
use_cases: a medieval feast scene in a film or a game
a menu for a historical banquet
a food image for a court of 1400

skills.name: Renaissance banquet
skills.thesis: Show the power of the host with the number, the skill and the beauty of the dishes, and let sugar and pastry take the shape of buildings and beasts.
skills.summary: The feast of the Italian court as Bartolomeo Scappi set it down in 1570. A kitchen of many cooks sends out many dishes at once: pies, roasts, candied fruit and sculpture in sugar. The cook uses the fork, the sugar and the spit with great skill.
use_cases: a menu for a historical dinner of the 16th century
a still life of a banquet table

skills.name: Cuisine françoise
skills.thesis: Cook for the taste of the food itself: build each sauce on a stock and a roux, and use herbs where the medieval kitchen used spice.
skills.summary: The French kitchen after La Varenne. Le Cuisinier françois of 1651 sets down the roux, the stock, the bouquet garni and fines herbes. Spice falls to pepper and nutmeg, and butter replaces lard. The flavour of the main food leads.
use_cases: a dinner scene at the court of Louis XIV
a menu for a historical French dinner
a food image of a 17th century sauce

skills.name: Grande cuisine
skills.thesis: Make cooking an art of order and show: a system of sauces on the stove, and architecture of sugar and pastry on the table.
skills.summary: The cuisine of the great houses as Marie-Antoine Carême wrote it. Four grand sauces form the base of a system. Pastry and sugar make a pièce montée that looks like a building. Many dishes stand on the table at once.
use_cases: a banquet scene of the early 19th century
a menu or a still life of a grand dinner
a sugar and pastry centrepiece design

skills.name: Cuisine classique
skills.thesis: Simplify Carême and make the kitchen a system: every dish comes from a small set of bases, cooked by a station that does one task.
skills.summary: The kitchen of the grand hotel as Auguste Escoffier set it down. A brigade of stations cooks a menu of courses from a fixed system of stocks and mother sauces, and serves each dish on its own plate. Le Guide culinaire of 1903 holds about 5,000 recipes of the system.
use_cases: a period dinner scene in a grand hotel
a menu for a classic French restaurant
a food photograph of a classic sauced dish

skills.name: Haute cuisine régionale
skills.thesis: Cook the classic dish well with the best produce of the region, on a short menu, and make the restaurant a place of travel.
skills.summary: The restaurant of a master in a provincial town. Fernand Point at La Pyramide in Vienne cooks the classic sauce with the butter, cream and produce of his own region. A small kitchen, a short menu and a fine cellar draw guests to the road.
use_cases: a scene in a French provincial restaurant of the 1950s
a menu for a regional classic dinner
a food image of a butter and cream dish

skills.name: Nouvelle cuisine
skills.thesis: Take the weight out of Escoffier: fresh market produce, short cooking and a sauce without flour let the taste of the ingredient lead.
skills.summary: A light French restaurant kitchen. The chef buys fresh produce at the market, cooks fish and vegetables for a short time, makes sauces without flour, and plates each dish in the kitchen. Gault and Millau gave it ten rules in 1973.
use_cases: a menu for a 1970s French restaurant
a food photograph of a small plated dish on a large white plate
a period scene of a chef at the pass

skills.name: California cuisine
skills.thesis: The best cooking starts with the best produce: buy ripe food from known growers in season, and then do as little to it as you can.
skills.summary: The kitchen of the local farm and the single daily menu. Alice Waters opened Chez Panisse in 1971 and cooked simple French dishes with produce from named growers, in season, with little change to the ingredient.
use_cases: a menu for a farm-to-table restaurant
a food photograph of a ripe salad on a rustic plate
a seasonal menu with the names of farms

skills.name: Cuisine minceur
skills.thesis: A dish can be low in fat and sugar and still be haute cuisine, if the cook uses exact technique and fresh produce in place of butter and cream.
skills.summary: Michel Guérard's light cooking for a spa hotel. Each dish has few calories but the plate of a three-star kitchen: steam instead of butter, fromage blanc and vegetable purée instead of cream and flour, and a small portion.
use_cases: a menu for a spa or wellness hotel
a food photograph of a light plate with a pale sauce
a diet menu that still looks like fine dining

skills.name: Naturalist cuisine
skills.thesis: The land around the kitchen is the pantry and the teacher: the cook walks it, learns each plant in each week, and cooks only what the walk gives.
skills.summary: A kitchen that treats the plate as a landscape. The cook picks wild and garden plants on the day, cooks each one at its own pace and shows it whole. The gargouillou of Michel Bras, first made in 1980, holds dozens of plants.
use_cases: a vegetable-led tasting menu of a country restaurant
a food photograph of a scattered plate of herbs and flowers
a menu that follows a walk in the landscape

skills.name: Pacific Rim fusion
skills.thesis: A chef from one tradition can use the pantry and the flavours of another, if the cook keeps the balance of each dish and the precision of the technique.
skills.summary: French technique and Californian produce with the sauces and the fish of Asia. Chinois on Main (1983), Roy's in Honolulu (1988) and Matsuhisa and Nobu from 1987 put soy, ginger, miso and raw fish on a plated menu.
use_cases: a menu for a fusion restaurant of the 1990s
a food photograph of seared fish with an Asian sauce
a sushi bar with a French plate

skills.name: Novoandina and Nikkei cuisine
skills.thesis: Peru holds the sea, the desert, the mountain and the jungle, and the cooks of Lima join them with the knives of Japan and the sauces of France to make one new national kitchen.
skills.summary: A kitchen of Lima that takes the potatoes, grains and chillies of the Andes and the fish of the Pacific, and gives them French and Japanese technique. Gastón Acurio, Virgilio Martínez and Mitsuharu Tsumura made it a world cuisine.
use_cases: a menu of ceviche, tiradito and Peruvian small dishes
a food photograph of raw fish with chilli and lime
a tasting menu by altitude of the Andes

skills.name: Molecular gastronomy
skills.thesis: Cooks can ask why food changes when it is heated, mixed or frozen, and then use the answer to build new textures, temperatures and surprises.
skills.summary: A kitchen that uses the science of food as a tool and a game. Hervé This and Nicholas Kurti named the field in 1988. Ferran Adrià at elBulli and Heston Blumenthal at The Fat Duck made foams, spheres and liquid-nitrogen ice cream.
use_cases: a tasting menu that plays with texture and temperature
a food photograph of a sphere, a foam or a frozen dish
a menu that tells a science story

skills.name: Bistronomie
skills.thesis: Good cooking does not need a palace: a trained chef can serve fine produce and exact technique in a simple room at a fair price.
skills.summary: A chef of a palace kitchen cooks at the price of a bistro. Yves Camdeborde opened La Régalade in Paris in 1992 with a fixed menu, honest produce, regional dishes and big portions, in a plain room with no linen and no ceremony.
use_cases: a menu for a Paris neighbourhood bistro
a food photograph of a braise in a cast-iron pot
a blackboard menu with a fixed price

skills.name: Modernist cuisine
skills.thesis: A cook who knows the physics of heat, water and texture can control the result to the degree, the second and the gram, and can then make food that was not possible before.
skills.summary: A kitchen that cooks by measurement and shows how it works. The six-volume book Modernist Cuisine of 2011 set out the physics of sous-vide, pressure, gels and freezing. Grant Achatz at Alinea in Chicago turned the method into a tasting menu.
use_cases: a tasting menu that states the time and the temperature of each dish
a food photograph of a clean plate with an exact cooked piece
a recipe book that shows the method and the physics

skills.name: New Nordic cuisine
skills.thesis: A kitchen of one place and one season: the cold, the short summer and the long winter of the North set the menu, and the cook preserves the summer for the winter.
skills.summary: A tasting-menu kitchen that cooks only what grows, swims or is foraged in the Nordic region, in the season of the day. Twelve chefs signed the Manifesto for the New Nordic Kitchen in 2004. Vinegar, ferments and wild plants replace lemon and olive oil.
use_cases: a tasting menu of a Nordic restaurant
a food photograph on dark stoneware
a menu that uses only local and seasonal produce

skills.name: Plant-based fine dining
skills.thesis: The top of the table does not need an animal: with skill, time and ferments, a carrot, a beet or a nut can carry the weight that foie gras and beef once carried.
skills.summary: A tasting-menu kitchen that uses no meat, fish, dairy, egg or honey. It gives the luxury of the old menu to vegetables, grains, nuts and ferments. Eleven Madison Park in New York changed to such a menu in 2021 under Daniel Humm, and put some animal products back in 2025.
use_cases: a vegan tasting menu of a formal restaurant
a food photograph of a single vegetable on a large plate
a menu that keeps luxury but removes animal products

origin.note: DJI sells the Phantom, a ready-to-fly drone that carries a small camera.

adoptions.via: Right Up Our Alley, a one-take FPV flight through a bowling alley, makes the drone a camera that flies through rooms.

origin.note: The PlayStation's graphics chip maps textures with no perspective correction.

adoptions.via: PlayStation games show warped floors and walls as a side effect of the hardware.
Haunted PS1 developers use shaders that copy the warp on purpose.

origin.note: Klaus Märtens founds a company on the patent of his air-cushioned sole.

adoptions.via: A Northamptonshire factory fits the air-cushioned sole to the eight-eye boot.

origin.note: Frank Rudy patents a sole with a sealed gas unit, and the first shoe appears in 1978.

adoptions.via: A running shoe is the first to carry the sealed air unit in its heel.
The Air Jordan 1 shows the air unit as a mark of the signed shoe.

origin.note: Abner Peeler patents a paint distributor; the airbrush of Charles Burdick (1893) goes into photo studios for retouch.

adoptions.via: Streamline posters and car advertisements use airbrushed gradients and chrome.
Illustrators airbrush surreal chrome, lightning and X-ray cut-aways for album covers and magazines.
Photoshop 1.0 ships with an airbrush tool, and the soft spray becomes digital.
Mac OS X 10.0 ships the Aqua interface, with gel buttons and scroll bars in soft gradients and one white highlight.
Web 2.0 logos take the airbrush gradient and the white specular highlight to the screen as glossy marks.
Apple Aqua icons in Mac OS X use soft gradients, highlights and cast shadows that echo airbrush work.
Glossy interface gradients and highlights take the airbrush look to the screen.
iPhone OS draws glass, chrome and felt with soft gradients and specular highlights.

origin.note: MS-DOS 2.0 loaded ANSI.SYS, which let a text screen set colour and cursor position with escape codes.

adoptions.via: Users of dial-up bulletin boards draw logos and menus with block characters and ANSI colour codes.

origin.note: Jean-Baptiste Le Prince made aquatints in 1768 to 1769; other makers also claim the invention.

adoptions.via: Francisco Goya publishes Los Caprichos with etched line and deep aquatint tones.

origin.note: Roman builders use the semicircular masonry arch at large scale in aqueducts, bridges and gates; the arch itself is older.

adoptions.via: Filippo Brunelleschi puts round Roman arches on slim columns in the loggia of the Foundling Hospital in Florence.
Palladian arched windows and niches frame Georgian rooms.
The Ecole des Beaux-Arts teaches the triumphal arch and the arcade as the main entrance of a public building; the Paris Opera opens in 1875.
Postmodern facades quote the round arch as a sign, not as a structure.
Bohemian websites frame photographs and cards in arch-shaped masks.
Arched mirrors, headboards, doorways and painted arches become a room motif.

origin.note: English works make glazed architectural faience for shops, pubs and public buildings.

adoptions.via: New York and Los Angeles works make glazed slabs in blue-green, cream and gold for Art Deco towers and cinemas.

origin.note: Ash falls on pots in a wood-fired kiln and melts into a thin green glaze.

adoptions.via: Hamada Shōji settles in Mashiko and mixes ash glazes from local plant ash and rock, and fires them in a wood-fired kiln.
Studio potters fire wood-ash and shino glazes on stoneware plates that they make with chefs.

origin.note: Harley Earl's styling section at General Motors uses clay to shape cars before the steel is cut.

adoptions.via: The fin and the wrap-around glass are first judged in clay.
Stylists check the long bonnet and the short deck in clay at full size.
Designers cut the flat planes and the sharp crease of the wedge in clay.
Designers model round, soft forms in clay for the small city car.
Designers copy the old forms in clay and then scale them up.

origin.note: Windows Vista Aero blurs what is behind the translucent frame of each window.

adoptions.via: iOS 7 puts the control centre and the menus on blurred, translucent layers.
CSS backdrop-filter reaches the main browsers, and web pages take up frosted panels.
Apple's Liquid Glass adds refraction and bright edges to the blurred layer.

origin.note: Eddie Bauer makes the first quilted goose-down jacket after a near-fatal trip in the cold.

adoptions.via: The Eddie Bauer shop sells the first quilted goose-down jacket.

origin.note: BBCode was first introduced in 1998 as a markup for message boards.

adoptions.via: phpBB 3.1 has a completely rewritten BBCode system for the posts on its boards.

origin.note: Madeleine Vionnet makes the bias cut the base of a whole line of gowns in the early 1920s.

adoptions.via: The Vionnet workroom cuts evening gowns on the bias; Hollywood costume houses copy the cut for the screen.

origin.note: Clement Ader sends stereo telephone sound from the Paris Opera to listeners at the Electrical Exhibition, an early use of two-channel sound.

adoptions.via: Close-mic video channels use binaural mics to make whispers and taps move between the ears.

origin.note: Half-Life 2: Lost Coast is made to show HDR rendering.

adoptions.via: Gears of War and other HD console games use bloom across whole scenes.
HD-2D games use bloom on lamps to make pixel scenes glow.

origin.note: Le Corbusier completes the Unité d'Habitation with walls and piers of raw, board-marked concrete.

adoptions.via: Loft interiors and restaurants cast board-marked concrete walls and counters.

origin.note: Thomas Frye patents a porcelain with bone ash at the Bow works.

adoptions.via: Josiah Spode II fixes a bone china recipe that Staffordshire potters then use for tea and dinner services.

origin.note: Boned bodices of linen and whalebone appear at the courts of Europe.

adoptions.via: Stay-makers cut linen stays with whalebone strips in sewn channels and shaped them into a cone.
Steel boning became popular and gave the corset a bone that springs back.
Designers put the boned bodice on the street as a top and a dress.

origin.note: Calvin Klein puts his name on the waistband of a plain cotton brief.

adoptions.via: The fashion house of Calvin Klein sold the named brief as fashion and advertised it on large posters.

origin.note: Le Viandier gives bread as the main binder of its sauces, as in the cameline sauce.

adoptions.via: Italian and French banquet kitchens kept bread as a binder beside the first butter sauces.

origin.note: Three engineers in Recife patent the cobogó, a hollow concrete block for screen walls in a hot climate.

adoptions.via: Tropical modernism and desert houses in the United States use screen walls; Edward Durell Stone wraps the US Embassy in New Delhi (1959) in a pierced screen.
Breeze-block room dividers, bar fronts and planters move inside the house.

origin.note: The pen is older than print; Gutenberg cut his textura from the broad-nib book hand of the scribes, the first record of the pen in type.

adoptions.via: Gutenberg's textura for the 42-line Bible copies the broken broad-nib hand.
Nicolas Jenson cuts a roman with the diagonal stress of the humanist broad-nib hand.
Edward Johnston, a calligrapher, draws the London Underground sans from broad-nib proportions.

origin.note: Antoni Gaudí and his team cover the benches and roofs of Park Güell with broken tile.

adoptions.via: Masons at Park Güell set shards of tile and plate on curved walls, benches and roof ridges.

origin.note: The first graphical browsers showed every page in the same default style, and artists treated that look as a material.

adoptions.via: Net artists use frames, raw text and links as the work, for example on the pages of Jodi.

origin.note: John Brooks sees English polo players pin their collars down, and he copies the idea for the shirt of his firm.

adoptions.via: College clothiers sell the oxford button-down as the base of the Ivy League look.

origin.note: Builders in northern Europe project the upper floors of timber houses beyond the lower floor on jetties.

adoptions.via: Frank Lloyd Wright carries the roofs of the Robie House 6 m past the wall on steel beams.
Mart Stam and then Marcel Breuer bend steel tube into a chair that has no back legs.
The studio block of the Bauhaus Dessau has a small cantilevered balcony at each studio.
The houses of the Weissenhof Estate in Stuttgart extend slabs past their columns, so that the window band can turn the corner.
Marcel Breuer puts the cantilever chair of bent steel tube into series production.
Wright cantilevers the concrete terraces of Fallingwater over a stream in Pennsylvania.
John Lautner pushes the roof of Googie's Coffee Shop far past its glass walls, and later roadside buildings copy the flying roof.
Verner Panton draws the Panton chair as a cantilever seat in one moulded shell.

origin.note: E. A. Johnson describes a capacitive touch screen at the Royal Radar Establishment.

adoptions.via: The Apple Watch puts a small touch screen on the face, with a digital crown to scroll.

origin.note: Instagram lets users share up to 10 photos and videos in one post.

adoptions.via: Users post casual camera-roll carousels that they call photo dumps.

origin.note: Smilebit's Jet Set Radio is the first widely known cel-shaded game.

adoptions.via: Studios render 3D vehicles and sets with toon shaders to match hand-drawn animation.

origin.note: German makers extrude hollow terracotta panels for hung, ventilated facades.

adoptions.via: Architects use extruded terracotta panels on rails for offices, schools and museums in northern Europe.

origin.note: S. Donald Stookey finds that a glass left in a furnace at too high a heat does not melt and turns opaque.

adoptions.via: Corning turns the process into cookware: pans of white glass-ceramic go from the freezer to a gas flame.

origin.note: The first firm records of the lime cure of fish are of the early nineteenth century in Lima.

adoptions.via: Gastón Acurio served ceviche as a fine-dining course at Astrid y Gastón in Lima.

origin.note: Jarkko Oikarinen writes Internet Relay Chat, with rooms called channels that start with #.

adoptions.via: Discord puts # text channels and voice channels in a server for each community.

origin.note: Squares of two colours of marble pave Italian church floors and palace halls.

adoptions.via: Leon Battista Alberti builds the perspective of a picture on a squared pavement in De pictura.
Black and white floors pave Art Deco halls, bars and bathrooms.
Dorothy Draper lays black-and-white marble floors in hotel lobbies and halls.
Checker rugs, tiles and painted floors become a motif of colourful rooms.

origin.note: The chefs of the nouvelle cuisine, among them the Troisgros brothers and Paul Bocuse, put the plating in the kitchen and not at the table.

adoptions.via: Michel Guérard set small steamed portions on wide plates for the guests of the spa.
Chinois on Main and later Roy's and Nobu plated an Asian main piece in a modern shape on a wide plate.

origin.note: Italian painters model form with strong light and dark from the late 15th century; Caravaggio makes the contrast extreme in The Calling of Saint Matthew (1599–1600).

adoptions.via: Caravaggio paints figures out of a dark ground with one hard shaft of light, and the Baroque painters follow.
Joseph Wright of Derby, and the Romantic painters after him, light night scenes from one candle, fire or moon.
Cecil B. DeMille and the cameraman Alvin Wyckoff light The Cheat with hard side light and call the result Rembrandt lighting.
The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari uses painted shadows and sharp light to set a mind in a distorted room.
Citizen Kane and The Maltese Falcon use low-key light, deep shadow and hard bars of light; crime films of the 1940s make it a house style.
Stills of noir films and press night photographs keep the single hard light and the black ground.
Blade Runner, shot by Jordan Cronenweth for Ridley Scott, cuts shafts of light through smoke and blinds in a colour city.
Dark academia photographs light a face or a book with one candle or window and let the rest fall into shadow.

origin.note: Louis XIV builds the Trianon de Porcelaine, with blue-and-white tiles after Chinese porcelain.

adoptions.via: François Boucher paints Chinese scenes for tapestries and decoration.
Grandmillennial rooms hang hand-painted chinoiserie wallpaper with birds and branches.

origin.note: Painted and printed Indian cottons reach Europe through the East India Companies.

adoptions.via: Victorian parlours cover sofas, curtains and walls in floral chintz.
Roller-printed cotton in strong floral patterns covers sofas, chairs and curtains in factory-made sets.
Grandmillennial rooms bring back chintz, skirted tables and floral wallpaper.

origin.note: Larry Butler makes the blue-screen travelling-matte shots of The Thief of Bagdad.

adoptions.via: TikTok adds a green-screen effect: the creator keeps the face and body and swaps the ground for any photo.

origin.note: Colin Fink and Charles Eldridge at Columbia University develop the bath that makes bright chromium coats.

adoptions.via: Chrome plate gives costume jewels a bright, cheap, white-metal shine.
Chrome replaces nickel on the radiator shell and the lamps of the grand car.
Chrome strips follow the flow of the body.
Bumpers, grilles and fins carry large amounts of chrome.
Chrome stays on the grille and the bumper of the muscle car.
Chrome returns on revived models as a sign of the past.

origin.note: Louis Moinet builds the first chronograph to time the stars.

adoptions.via: The Speedmaster carries two pushers, three sub dials and a tachymeter bezel, to time laps and measure speed.

origin.note: Eadweard Muybridge records a galloping horse with a row of cameras; Étienne-Jules Marey takes many exposures on one plate from 1882.

adoptions.via: Étienne-Jules Marey makes his chronophotographic gun and fixed plate in Paris.
Anton Giulio Bragaglia publishes photodynamism, a blurred photograph of movement.
Giacomo Balla paints Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash with repeated legs and tail.
Marcel Duchamp paints Nude Descending a Staircase No. 2 in stages.

origin.note: Designers fit clay cylinders to small 3D printers and print vessels in ceramic paste.

adoptions.via: Designers print vases with visible layer lines and fire them as plain earthenware, stoneware or porcelain.

origin.note: Early films such as The Sculptor's Nightmare animate figures modelled in clay.

adoptions.via: Icon sets render each object in 3D with one matte, clay-like material and soft light.
Claymorphism gives cards and buttons the round, puffed form of clay.

origin.note: Louis Anquetin and Émile Bernard paint flat, outlined shapes in Paris; the critic Édouard Dujardin names the manner in 1888.

adoptions.via: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, a friend of Anquetin and Bernard, prints flat fields of colour with a dark outline in the lithograph poster Moulin Rouge: La Goulue.

origin.note: Coach makers build horse-drawn carriages on a wood frame with leather and brass fittings. Early car bodies copy this work.

adoptions.via: The first cars carry carriage bodies on wood frames, with brass lamps and leather seats.
Coachbuilders make one-off bodies on bought chassis, and the client chooses the line, the colour and the trim.
Turin works beat light alloy bodies by hand for small series of grand tourers.

origin.note: Louis Vuitton covers the flat-topped trunk in grey lacquered canvas; it is light, weatherproof and does not crack as leather does.

adoptions.via: The Vuitton workshop adds a stripe to the coated canvas, the first pattern on a trunk.
Luxury houses print a mark across the whole coated canvas of bags and belts.

origin.note: Jingdezhen potters make blue-and-white porcelain with imported cobalt.

adoptions.via: Jingdezhen kilns paint porcelain with cobalt for the Yuan court and the export trade.
Iznik potters copy Chinese blue-and-white and paint cobalt on a white stonepaste body.
Jingdezhen potters paint panelled dishes in cobalt blue for export to Portugal and, later, the Dutch Republic.

origin.note: Alphonse Poitevin invented and patented the process in 1855.

adoptions.via: Joseph Albert and Jakub Husník make a gelatin plate on glass, and Albert builds the first mechanised collotype press.
Eadweard Muybridge publishes Animal Locomotion with 781 plates printed as collotypes.

origin.note: Mario Bava lights Blood and Black Lace with red, green and blue gels; colour light is older in the theatre and in colour film.

adoptions.via: Mario Bava uses gelled light in Blood and Black Lace and sets the look of the giallo.
Dario Argento and the cameraman Luciano Tovoli light Suspiria with saturated gels and print it on dye-transfer Technicolor.
Nicolas Winding Refn bathes Only God Forgives in red and blue light.

origin.note: Sanitary firms make flat in-wall cisterns, so that the wall can hide the water tank of a WC.

adoptions.via: Designers use the frame to hang the WC on the wall, so that the bowl floats and the floor stays clear.

origin.note: Albrecht Duerer publishes letters built with ruler and compass on a square grid in Underweysung der Messung.

adoptions.via: The committee of the Academie des Sciences draws the Romain du roi on a grid of 2304 small squares.
Herbert Bayer draws the Universal alphabet at the Bauhaus with a compass and a ruler.
Paul Renner draws Futura from the circle, the square and the triangle.
Otl Aicher builds the pictograms of the Munich Olympics on a grid with angles of 45° and 90° only.
The Twitter bird is drawn from overlapping circles with set radii.
Material Design sets 24 dp icons with a 20 dp live area and keyline shapes.

origin.note: Jacob Davis rivets the pocket corners of work trousers, and the patent that he shares with Levi Strauss follows on 20 May 1873.

adoptions.via: The factory of Levi Strauss in San Francisco makes the riveted waist overall in denim and duck.

origin.note: Jōmon potters press cord into the wet wall of the first Japanese pots.

adoptions.via: Jōmon potters mark the whole wall of a deep pot with cord and name the period after the pattern.

origin.note: Herminie Cadolle files a patent for a corset that is cut into a lower corset and an upper bust support.

adoptions.via: Mary Phelps Jacob patented a light backless brassière of two handkerchiefs and ribbon, with no corset.
A maker of brassières founded in 1922 sold the separate bust support in sizes.

origin.note: Embroidery houses of Paris, such as the Lesage atelier of 1924, make beading a craft of couture; bead embroidery itself is much older.

adoptions.via: The Baguette bag is covered in hand-sewn beads and sequins, and each colourway takes days of work.

origin.where: Horta de Ebro, La Roche-Guyon and Paris

Pavel Janak and Josef Gocar design Czech Cubist buildings with faceted walls, such as the House of the Black Madonna in Prague.
Bruno Taut builds the Glass Pavilion for the Werkbund exhibition in Cologne as a crystal dome of glass prisms.
Hermann Warm, Walter Reimann and Walter Roehrig build the angled, painted sets of The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari.
The MoMA exhibition Deconstructivist Architecture shows broken and tilted planes by Gehry, Hadid and Libeskind.

Norman Foster hangs a frameless glass wall from the roof of the Willis Faber and Dumas building in Ipswich.
