Marinid builders in Fez and Meknes cut glazed tiles into small stars and polygons for walls and fountains.

origin.note: Adobe releases Photoshop 1.0, which makes layered cut-outs a desktop task.

adoptions.via: Product cut-outs on white form the cells of the starter pack collage.
Meme makers place cut-outs at odd scale in surreal memes.

origin.note: Tea master Furuta Oribe orders bent, square and lopsided tea ware from the Mino kilns.

adoptions.via: Mino potters press the rims and walls out of true to make each piece look alive.

origin.note: Kazimir Malevich shows tilted, floating shapes in Suprematist paintings at the exhibition 0.10.

adoptions.via: El Lissitzky draws Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge: a red wedge cuts into a white circle.
Aleksandr Rodchenko sets the lines of his posters, such as the Books ad, on strong diagonals.
Sergei Eisenstein stages frames of Battleship Potemkin along strong diagonals.
Jan Tschichold teaches the asymmetric, diagonal page in Die neue Typographie.

origin.note: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and co-authors publish the first diffusion method for images; it is a paper in machine learning.

adoptions.via: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel publish Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.
Midjourney and DALL-E 2 put text-to-image models in the hands of illustrators and designers.
Stable Diffusion releases its weights in August, and its glossy default look spreads as a recognisable image style.
A free low-resolution model, DALL-E Mini, makes 3x3 grids of smudged images that users share as jokes.
Open models and photo apps make the stylised avatar pack; the Lensa Magic Avatars feature spreads it in December.
The default output of text-to-image models, with a rim light, bokeh and a teal and amber grade, becomes a known look.
Mass-made generated images fill social feeds with bait captions; the word slop names them.

origin.note: Tile factories change from roller and screen printing to inkjet printing in the early 2000s.

adoptions.via: Italian and Spanish tile factories print stone and wood images on porcelain stoneware with ceramic inks.

origin.note: O Brother, Where Art Thou? is the first feature film that is graded as a whole in a digital intermediate.

adoptions.via: Photographers apply film-look presets and split toning in Lightroom to push skin to orange and shadows to teal.

origin.note: The Vacublitz flash bulb replaces flash powder and makes the flash safe to use by hand.

adoptions.via: Compact digital cameras fire their small built-in flash at each snapshot.
Party and nightlife photographers post direct-flash pictures from clubs to blogs.
Night photographs of empty corridors and car parks use on-camera flash or a flat lamp with a cheap camera look.

origin.note: The Mainz Psalter of Fust and Schöffer prints large decorated initials in red and blue.

adoptions.via: Victorian books and magazines open chapters with engraved, ornamented initials.
Editorial sites open long articles with a large serif initial over 3 to 4 lines.

origin.note: The Housebook Master, a south German artist, seems to have invented it; all his prints are in drypoint.

adoptions.via: Rembrandt prints The Three Crosses in heavy drypoint, with a thick burr in the dark areas.
Mary Cassatt shows colour prints in Paris that she makes with drypoint and aquatint.

origin.note: BeReal releases an app that asks users to post a back and a front camera photo at a random time.

adoptions.via: BeReal grows fast, and its two-camera snapshot becomes a common look in social feeds.

origin.note: Designers on Dribbble post soft-plastic interface concepts, and the name neumorphism spreads.

adoptions.via: Claymorphism adds an inner shadow and a large radius, so that cards look like soft clay.

origin.note: Richard Prosser takes out a patent for pressing tiles from clay dust, and Minton uses it for floor tiles.

adoptions.via: Minton and other Staffordshire firms press floor tiles from dust in a steel die, and the tiles have square, even edges.
New York tile works press small white wall tiles from dust, with bevelled edges and ribs on the back.

origin.note: Animators draw more frames at the start and the end of a move; Thomas and Johnston name it slow in and slow out.

adoptions.via: Robert Penner publishes easing equations for Flash, and web motion takes them up.
CSS transitions define timing functions such as ease-in-out and cubic-bezier().

origin.note: Wolfgang Puck opened Chinois on Main and cooked French and Californian dishes with Chinese flavours.

adoptions.via: Roy Yamaguchi opened Roy's in Honolulu and cooked European technique with the produce and the sauces of Asia and the Pacific.

origin.note: Joseph Sparkes Hall makes elastic-sided boots, and Queen Victoria wears them.

adoptions.via: The elastic-sided boot enters the mass market, and the gusset becomes a mark of the Victorian boot.

origin.note: George and Henry Elkington patent cyanide silver plating; Luigi Brugnatelli gilded silver by electrolysis in 1805.

adoptions.via: Elkington silver plate replaces Sheffield plate on factory-made tableware.
Gilt and chrome plate give cast base-metal jewels the look of gold and platinum.
Nickel and chrome plate cover the lamps, the radiator and the bumpers of the car.
Nickel-plated brass and chrome-plated steel become the metal of the modern lamp and chair.
Silver plate and chrome stay on Nordic tableware and lamps next to stainless steel.

origin.note: Craftsmen cut patterns on a rose engine lathe in wood, ivory and soft metal.

adoptions.via: Josiah Wedgwood buys a rose engine lathe to cut fine patterns in the leather-hard body of his wares.
Potters turn sharp bands and patterns in slip on the leather-hard pot with a lathe, in the way that a watchmaker or an ornamental turner cuts metal.
Breguet cuts engine-turned patterns of lines and waves in the gold or silver dial of a watch.
Deco watch dials of silver and gold carry engine-turned patterns, sometimes under clear enamel.
The dial of the Royal Oak carries a grid pattern in the manner of engine turning, called the tapisserie.

origin.note: Urs Graf makes the first dated etching, on an iron plate. Daniel Hopfer etched prints from about 1500, and armourers used acid to decorate metal before that.

adoptions.via: Rembrandt etches portraits, scenes and landscapes beside his painting and makes the etching a painter's medium.

origin.note: Egyptian carpenters lock the parts of chairs, beds and chests with mortise-and-tenon joints and leave the joints in view.

adoptions.via: Shaker joiners show dovetails and tenons on plain chests and chairs.
Shaker workshops make chairs, chests and boxes with dovetails and tenons in view.
Ernest Gimson and the Barnsley brothers make oak furniture with pegged tenons and plain joints in the Cotswolds.
Gustav Stickley sells Craftsman furniture with through-tenons that show on the face.
Greene and Greene build the Gamble House in Pasadena with pegged and exposed timber joints.
Sori Yanagi joins the two bent plywood shells of the Butterfly stool with one brass rod that stays in view.
Peter Zumthor and other critical regionalists keep the joint and the junction as the only ornament.
Craft makers leave dovetails and pegs in view on solid oak tables and cabinets.
Japandi rooms show the joints of oak and ash furniture, as Japanese and Danish joiners do.

origin.note: The Centre Pompidou of Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers puts its ducts, pipes and escalators on the outside.

adoptions.via: Loft conversions leave ducts, pipes and cable trays bare on the ceiling.

origin.note: George Albert Smith inserts magnified close views into Grandma's Reading Glass.

adoptions.via: Carl Theodor Dreyer fills the frame with the face of Renée Falconetti in The Passion of Joan of Arc.
Sergio Leone cuts between the eyes of gunmen and a wide desert in A Fistful of Dollars, on a Techniscope 2.35:1 frame.
Chuck Close paints a huge frontal head from a photograph in Big Self-Portrait (1967–68).
Goblincore photographs fill the frame with a mushroom cap, a moss patch or a snail shell.

origin.note: A user of that name posts the first face-swap clips and then shares the method as code; the name deepfake comes from this user name.

adoptions.via: Open tools and phone apps put the method in many hands; detection overlays and labels appear next to the clips.

origin.note: Apple releases Animoji with the iPhone X and its TrueDepth camera.

adoptions.via: Animoji and later Memoji turn the face of the user into a rendered mask in messages and video.

origin.note: Kizuna AI uses a tracked 3D avatar as the host of a YouTube channel, and other makers follow the same rig.

adoptions.via: Virtual YouTubers use tracked anime-style avatars as live hosts.

origin.note: Alexander Mordvintsev and colleagues post the method and its first images in a Google research blog in June 2015.

adoptions.via: Google releases the code in July 2015; users post dog-face and eye-filled photographs on web forums and image boards.

origin.note: Scheduling apps add a grid preview of the Instagram profile.

adoptions.via: Brand and creator profiles plan the grid as one board with a repeat rhythm.

origin.note: Late works of Michelangelo and the painters after him twist figures in a spiral; Lomazzo names the idea in 1584.

adoptions.via: El Greco stretches and twists his figures in tall altarpieces in Toledo.

origin.note: The silk trade of Lyon grows from the royal privilege that Francis I gives to the city in 1536.

adoptions.via: Lyon mills weave light flower brocades for the Rococo gowns of the French court.

origin.note: The Sholes and Glidden typewriter by E. Remington and Sons moves the carriage one fixed step for each key, so its type must be monospaced.

adoptions.via: Typewriter faces, then Courier for IBM in 1955.
Video terminals such as the DEC VT100 draw the whole screen as a grid of 80 by 24 character cells.
Brutalist websites set all text in a system monospace face on default browser styles.

origin.note: Andrew Kromelow, a worker at Frank Gehry's studio, names the habit of laying objects at right angles knolling in 1987.

adoptions.via: Instagram users post overhead photos of coffee, notebooks and flowers on pale surfaces.

origin.note: The Troisgros brothers made salmon with a sorrel sauce that the cook did not thicken with starch.

adoptions.via: Michel Guérard cut the butter and the cream further and bound his sauces with fromage blanc and vegetable purée.

origin.note: Greek Doric and Ionic columns carry vertical concave grooves; a Doric shaft has 20 flutes.

adoptions.via: Jacques-Germain Soufflot gives the Pantheon in Paris, begun in 1764, a portico of fluted Corinthian columns.
Wedgwood and Boulton copy classical urns and columns, and the cabinet makers of the pattern books turn flutes on slim mahogany legs.
Neoclassical and Regency furniture takes fluted and reeded legs and friezes.
Art Deco rooms use fluted pilasters, fluted glass and fluted wood panels.
Reeded glass and fluted wood or stone cover cabinets, islands and walls.

origin.note: Forum users copy the black frame of the demotivational poster and change its text.

adoptions.via: Poster generators and forums make the framed template a one-click form.

origin.note: William Cotton patents a frame that knits panels to shape with the stitches fashioned on the edge.

adoptions.via: Cashmere houses such as Brunello Cucinelli link fully fashioned panels by hand, so that the fine knit has flat seams.

origin.note: Massimo Osti dyes made-up garments in a drum for his labels.

adoptions.via: Techwear labels dye the whole shell and trouser black, so that the cloth, the thread and the tape match.

origin.note: Issey Miyake begins to work on garment pleating, a process that keeps the pleats of polyester fixed after the cut.

adoptions.via: The Pleats Please line of Issey Miyake sells heat-set pleated polyester dresses and tops.

origin.note: Ian Goodfellow and co-authors publish the method in a paper in machine learning.

adoptions.via: NVIDIA releases StyleGAN; the next year a web page shows one new generated face on each reload.

origin.note: CompuServe releases the GIF format with support for several frames in one file.

adoptions.via: Tumblr users and later Giphy cut film and TV clips into short loops and send them as replies.
Net artists run glitch effects inside short loops of 20 to 40 frames.

origin.note: Owens-Corning makes glass fibre in quantity, and the first glass-fibre shells follow in the 1940s.

adoptions.via: Makers mould the sharp wedge body in glass fibre for short runs.

origin.note: Tang kilns make sancai tomb figures and vessels with running lead glazes in amber, green and cream.

adoptions.via: Kilns at Gongxian and near Chang'an splash three lead glazes on horses, camels and court ladies for tombs.

origin.note: Builders of Nebuchadnezzar II face the Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way with moulded and glazed bricks.

adoptions.via: Babylonian builders glaze moulded bricks in blue, white and yellow and set them in rows of lions, bulls and dragons.

origin.note: Chinese builders glaze roof tiles in the first centuries of the imperial age.

adoptions.via: Imperial kilns near Beijing make yellow, green and blue glazed tile for the roofs of the Forbidden City.

origin.note: Nam June Paik bends the picture of television sets with magnets in his first Exposition of Music-Electronic Television.

adoptions.via: Rosa Menkman writes the Glitch Studies Manifesto; designers copy channel splits and torn bands in posters and sites.
Short films and music videos shot on old camcorders keep VHS tracking errors and colour bleed.
Glitchcore edits split colour channels, repeat frames and add datamosh on fast cuts.
Cybercore pages add scan lines, split colour channels and torn frames as decoration.

origin.note: Apple showed the Aqua interface with glossy, drop-like buttons in January 2000.

adoptions.via: Web start-ups copy the gloss for buttons, badges and logos.

origin.note: Painters at the imperial kilns start to use an enamel of gold from Europe to make pink and its tints.

adoptions.via: Painters at Jingdezhen and in the palace workshops paint rose, flesh and petal tints on white porcelain in the Yongzheng and Qianlong years.
Sèvres painters fire a pink enamel of gold, later called rose Pompadour, on soft-paste porcelain.

origin.note: Charles Goodyear Jr. builds a machine that sews the welt.

adoptions.via: English makers in Northampton take the machine, and it sets the standard of the welted dress shoe.
The eight-eye workboot uses a welted sole with a yellow thread.

origin.note: Leon Battista Alberti describes a veil of threads that gives a grid over the scene in De pictura.

adoptions.via: Albrecht Dürer prints draughtsmen who draw through a frame with a grid in Underweysung der Messung.
Chuck Close works from a gridded photograph in Big Self-Portrait.

origin.note: Benjamin Day patents a mechanical tint of dots for printers; photographic halftone screens follow in the 1880s.

adoptions.via: The Daily Graphic of New York prints a photograph as a halftone.
State printers in Moscow copy the pasted montages through a coarse screen, so that photographs print in 2–4 flat inks.
Roy Lichtenstein paints enlarged Ben-Day dots by hand in Look Mickey.
Andy Warhol has photographs made into halftone screens and pulls them over hand-cut flat colour.
Punk zines photocopy halftones until the dots break up.
Duotone icon sets print each glyph in two tones of one hue, as a two-screen duotone does in print.

origin.note: The oldest fired pots, which are more than 10000 years old, are hand-built because the wheel is not yet known.

adoptions.via: Californian sculptors build large glazed figures and objects by hand, and keep thumb marks and cracks as part of the joke.

origin.note: London tailors of the Regency build the coat on canvas, so that the plain cloth shows a clean chest.

adoptions.via: The Savile Row houses make full-canvas coats to measure for the clubs and the court.

origin.note: World of Warcraft makes hand-painted, diffuse-only textures the standard of its art team.

adoptions.via: Torchlight and League of Legends carry the hand-painted look to other studios and to mobile games.

origin.note: Jean Rouch and Edgar Morin shoot Chronique d'un été with the light synchronous-sound camera that Michel Brault operates by hand; earlier handheld shots exist.

adoptions.via: Raoul Coutard shoots À bout de souffle by hand for Jean-Luc Godard.
Rouch, Brault and the Direct Cinema crews carry the light 16mm camera and the sound recorder into real rooms.
Easy Rider and other New Hollywood films use light cameras on real roads and locations.
The Dogme 95 Vow of Chastity demands that the camera is hand-held.
The Blair Witch Project gives the camera to its characters and shows the shake as their fear.
Andrew Bujalski shoots Funny Ha Ha with a small camera in plain rooms.
Sean Baker shoots Tangerine on three iPhone 5S phones with a clip-on anamorphic lens and a small stabiliser.
Camcorder revival films shoot on handheld consumer video cameras.
POV clips hold the phone at eye level and let the actor look at the lens.

origin.note: London type founders cast shaded and shadowed display letters for posters and handbills.

adoptions.via: Neo-brutalist interfaces give each card and button a solid black shadow offset by 4 to 8 px.

origin.note: Hatters block felt on carved wood blocks long before the Victorian trade; the method scales up with the many hat shapes of the 19th century.

adoptions.via: Victorian milliners block felt and straw bodies for each season's bonnet and hat shape.

origin.note: English makers in Lambeth and Staffordshire start to sell pressed terracotta blocks for buildings.

adoptions.via: Makers in London and Leeds press hollow terracotta blocks for museums, schools and town halls.
Chicago works make thin, hollow terracotta tile that hangs on the steel frame of a tall building.

origin.note: Netscape Navigator 1.1 added table support, and designers used tables for page layout.

adoptions.via: Web portals place search, links, news and ads in dense table grids.

origin.note: Forum users put white outlined Impact text on photos; the format spreads from imageboards.

adoptions.via: Imageboards and meme sites make the captioned photo a standard form.
Meme makers copy the bold caption into loud, recompressed pictures.
Meme makers put text labels on the people and objects of a stock photo to name their roles.

origin.note: John Wesley Hyatt patents a machine that presses hot celluloid into a mould.

adoptions.via: Moulded plastic forms the dashboard and the trim of the pony car.
Moulded plastic forms the dashboard and the black trim of the wedge.
The Swatch case and strap are moulded in plastic, so that the factory needs few parts and little hand work.
Large bumpers and panels are moulded in one piece and painted in the body colour.
Moulded plastic forms the smooth dash and the door cards.

origin.note: The Boston Watch Company builds a factory for machine-made watches.

adoptions.via: The Waltham firm makes watches with machine-cut parts and sells them at a price that railroad workers can pay.

origin.note: Potters at the Ding kilns start to fire bowls upside down on their rims.

adoptions.via: Ding potters stack thin bowls rim-down in stepped saggar rings and bind the bare rims with metal.

origin.note: William Farish publishes isometrical perspective as a method for engineering drawing.

adoptions.via: Theo van Doesburg and Cornelis van Eesteren show houses in axonometric drawings.
Sega's Zaxxon is the first arcade game in an isometric view.
Ultimate's Knight Lore builds rooms as isometric boxes on home computers.
Monument Valley uses an orthographic isometric view for impossible architecture.
Isometric illustrations show products, data and offices on tech pages.
Icon packs for product pages and dashboards draw small objects on the isometric grid.

origin.note: Whitby workshops begin to turn local jet into beads and ornaments.

adoptions.via: After the death of Prince Albert, jet jewels become the dress of court mourning, and the Whitby trade grows.

origin.note: Joseon potters throw large round jars in two halves and join them.

adoptions.via: Joseon potters make the large white moon jar in two bowls joined at the belly.

origin.note: The JPEG format becomes the usual lossy image format of the web; repeated saves show visible loss.

adoptions.via: Reddit and Tumblr users recompress pictures on purpose and make the damage the joke.

origin.note: Jean-Luc Godard cuts inside continuous shots in À bout de souffle and does not hide the jump.

adoptions.via: MTV starts in 1981; music videos cut on the beat and jump inside one take.
Video bloggers on YouTube cut the pauses out of a talk to the camera.
Gameplay commentary cuts every pause over 1.5 seconds and adds a sound hit.
Video essays cut pauses and hold each clip for 4 to 10 seconds, with the voice over the cut.
Musical.ly clips cut on the beat and loop at 15 seconds.
Vertical short-form apps make the fast jump cut the default rhythm of a clip.
Get-ready-with-me clips cut out each pause between outfit and make-up steps.

origin.note: The stencil craft grew in Ise in the Edo period. The date is the start of that period and not a firm record of a first stencil.

adoptions.via: The cutters of Shiroko and Jike in Ise supply stencils to the dyers of Japan for repeat patterns on cloth.

origin.note: Ken Burns pans and zooms over still photographs in a documentary series; rostrum-camera moves are older.

adoptions.via: Apple names the pan-and-zoom setting after Burns in its photo and video software.
Video essays move a slow zoom of 3% to 6% over a still or a clip.
Photo-mode slideshows zoom and pan slowly over each still image.

origin.note: Escoffier organised the hotel kitchen into parties, so that a dish was ready in minutes, not hours.

adoptions.via: Nouvelle cuisine kept the stations and gave the plating to the chef at the pass.

origin.note: Salted and soured vegetables were stored in China in the last centuries BCE; the method spread over Asia and Europe.

adoptions.via: The cooks of the Nordic kitchen, led by Noma, made ferments of vegetables, fruit and grain a part of the menu.
The plant-based menu of Eleven Madison Park used ferments in place of meat and dairy for depth of taste.

origin.note: Otto Hetzer patents glued laminated timber beams for halls and bridges.

adoptions.via: Alvar Aalto designs the Paimio chair with a frame of bent laminated birch.
Alvar Aalto makes the Paimio armchair with a frame of bent laminated birch, and Nordic workshops copy the method.
Charles and Ray Eames put moulded plywood chairs into mass production.
Charles and Ray Eames mould plywood into chair shells with compound curves for a large series.
Austrian researchers develop cross-laminated timber panels, and builders adopt them for floors and walls.
Waugh Thistleton builds Murray Grove in London, a 9-storey block with a CLT frame.

origin.note: The Adamson Brothers, part of the US Rubber Company, bring Lastex to the market.

adoptions.via: Makers of girdles and brassières used elastic yarn of rubber core to give the held waist of the new line.

origin.note: Factories in the Westerwald region start to sell vases with a thick, bubbling volcanic glaze.

adoptions.via: West German factories fire heavy vases in thick, cratered glazes of orange, brown and black.

origin.note: Longquan potters build a thick celadon glaze from several coats.

adoptions.via: Longquan kilns put a thick, jade-like glaze on the body in several coats.

origin.note: Celluloid starts to replace horn and tortoiseshell in spectacle frames; it is cheap, it polishes and it takes a tortoiseshell pattern.

adoptions.via: The browline frame joins a heavy plastic bar to a thin metal rim, and the cat-eye layers colours on the upper edge.

origin.note: The Everest party wears silk, wool and a gabardine smock in layers, and the climber adds or sheds one at each rest.

adoptions.via: The Everest party wears layers of silk, wool and a windproof gabardine smock.
Nordic walkers take a wool base, a mid layer and a waxed shell as one fixed kit.
Gorpcore takes the trail layers into the city and shows each layer in a different colour.

origin.note: Johannes Gutenberg prints the 42-line Bible from cast metal type in a screw press.

adoptions.via: Poster printers set large wood letters in the same press as metal type and print show bills by the hundred.
The press of Antonio Vanegas Arroyo prints the metal-plate pictures of José Guadalupe Posada with set type on one sheet (about 1890).
William Morris returns to the hand press, handmade paper and a heavy cast type at the Kelmscott Press.
Newspaper comics print from line plates and type on rotary letterpress, with Ben-Day tints on the colour plates.

origin.note: Carvers cut the spaced roman capitals of the inscription on Trajan's Column.

adoptions.via: Badges of clubs, railways and makers set the name in spaced capitals round the ring.
Fashion and hotel houses set their names in spaced roman capitals.
Carol Twombly draws the Trajan typeface for Adobe from the column inscription.
Luxury sites set spaced small-cap labels over a large serif head.

origin.note: Builders at Ain Ghazal coat floors and walls with burnt lime plaster; Catalhoyuk later paints its plastered walls.

adoptions.via: Le Corbusier records the white lime-washed houses of the Aegean on his Journey to the East.
Geoffrey Bawa builds white-plastered houses in Sri Lanka.
Beach houses in the USA put white-washed walls and boards in summer rooms.
Wabi-sabi websites use limewash and plaster textures as the page ground.

origin.note: Goldsmiths engrave copper plates and print them as pictures; the method then spreads across Europe.

adoptions.via: Martin Schongauer signs his copper engravings with a monogram; Dürer and Goltzius then take the burin line to its limit.
Print shops in Moscow and Kyiv engrave picture sheets on copper plates; the sheets are coloured by hand and sold as lubok.
George Bickham engraves the copperplate hands of The Universal Penman (1741) on copper.
John Baskerville has John Handy cut sharp, high-contrast roman type in Birmingham, and prints it on smooth wove paper.
Firmin Didot cuts roman type with hairline serifs and a vertical stress; Giambattista Bodoni follows in Parma.
Robert Thorne cuts fat faces that push the engraved contrast of the Didones to an extreme.
Jacob Perkins moves to London and engraves bank notes on hardened steel plates.
The UK Trade Marks Registration Act starts a register, and firms file engraved vignettes, banners and shaded figures.
Narbut draws pen lines in the manner of Baroque engraved books, and a zinc line block prints them.

origin.note: Paco Rabanne shows 12 Unwearable Dresses in Contemporary Materials, made of plastic discs and metal rings.

adoptions.via: Paco Rabanne links plastic and aluminium discs into short dresses, and the Space Age couture takes metal as a cloth.

origin.note: Artists of Die Brücke cut linoleum from about 1905. Vojtěch Preissig also made linoleum prints in 1911, in New York.

adoptions.via: Claude Flight and his group hold the first exhibition of British linocuts at the Redfern Gallery in London.
The Taller de Gráfica Popular opens in Mexico City and makes political prints from linoleum and wood blocks.

origin.note: Alois Senefelder invents lithography in Bavaria.

adoptions.via: A press in Tabriz prints the first lithographed Qur'an (AH 1248), and Iranian presses then print books from scribe-written stones.
Honoré Daumier draws crayon lithographs for Le Charivari in Paris.
Jules Chéret prints his first colour posters on his own presses in Paris, with one stone for each ink.
Odilon Redon publishes the lithographs of Dans le rêve, black dream visions.
Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec prints the poster Moulin Rouge: La Goulue in colour lithography.
Raja Ravi Varma founds the Ravi Varma Press and prints oleographs of his paintings from limestone and metal plates.
Edvard Munch prints The Scream as a lithograph.
The state printing works in St Petersburg prints Bilibin's fairy-tale books, with the tints drawn on separate stones.
Shanghai advertisers have yuefenpai calendar posters printed by chromolithography from rubbed charcoal and watercolour originals.
San Francisco poster artists have their dance posters printed by offset lithography, the planographic process on a rotary press.

origin.note: Online groups on Weirdcore and Liminalspace collect poor photos of empty rooms and playgrounds.

adoptions.via: Weirdcore posts use poor photos of empty places, with red text and black voids.
Dreamcore images use the same soft, degraded photos, with pastel colour and bloom.

origin.note: Giorgio de Chirico paints empty squares with long raking shadows in The Mystery and Melancholy of a Street.

adoptions.via: F. W. Murnau casts the shadow of the vampire on the stairs in Nosferatu.
Surrealist painters take over the empty, shadowed scene of de Chirico.
Flat design adds a 45° long shadow to icons and buttons.
Surreal web scenes use long shadows on calm, empty grounds.

origin.note: Alfred Hitchcock shoots Rope in takes of about 10 minutes, the length of one reel, and hides each join in a dark back or a close shape.

adoptions.via: Orson Welles opens Touch of Evil with a single crane and tracking shot of about three minutes.
Béla Tarr cuts Sátántangó into 150 shots in 7 hours, many of them takes of several minutes.
Alexander Sokurov makes Russian Ark as one Steadicam take of 96 minutes through the Hermitage.
Birdman, shot by Emmanuel Lubezki, hides its cuts to look like one take.
1917, shot by Roger Deakins, joins a few long takes into the look of one shot.

origin.note: Metalworkers cast small copper objects from a wax model.

adoptions.via: Studio jewellers cast silver and gold from their own wax models, in runs of a few pieces.
London jewellers cast gold from rough models, so that the surface looks like rock or bark.

origin.note: The Radium Luminous Material Corporation starts to sell luminous paint.

adoptions.via: A radium paint dial makes a wristwatch that soldiers read in the dark of the trench.
The pilot watch carries large numerals and hands filled with luminous paint for the night cockpit.
The diver watch carries large luminous markers, so that the diver reads it in dark water.

origin.note: Potters of Basra paint metal pigments on tin-glazed pots and fire them in smoke to make a gold sheen.

adoptions.via: William De Morgan tests lustre in Chelsea and makes ruby and gold lustre tiles and vases in London.

origin.note: Abbasid potters make the first lustre on glazed pots.

adoptions.via: Abbasid potters paint bowls and tiles with lustre in brown, gold and olive.
Moorish potters in Malaga and Valencia bring lustre to Spain and make it a trade ware.

origin.note: Paul Bocuse and the chefs of nouvelle cuisine bought produce at the market and built the menu from it.

adoptions.via: Alice Waters served one set menu at Chez Panisse that changed each day with the produce of local farms.
Yves Camdeborde wrote a fixed menu on a blackboard at La Régalade and changed it with the market.

origin.note: Graphic matches are older; the reference case is Stanley Kubrick's cut from a thrown bone to a satellite in orbit.

adoptions.via: Material motion in Android 5.0 carries one element from screen to screen as a shared-element transition.

origin.note: Expired and cross-processed film gives lifted blacks and tinted shadows in zine photos of the 1990s.

adoptions.via: Tumblr blogs reblog faded, pastel-tinted photos with lifted blacks and grain.
VSCO presets bring the matte lifted-black grade to phone photos.

origin.note: The Grueby Faience Company sells vases with a thick matt green glaze and moulded leaves.

adoptions.via: Grueby and then Rookwood, Newcomb and others sell vases in a velvet matt glaze, with leaf and flower reliefs.
The Steubenville Pottery sprays soft matt and satin glazes in grey, sea green and cinnamon on American Modern.

origin.note: W. L. Gore and Associates sells the first garment cloth with a stretched PTFE membrane.

adoptions.via: Gore-Tex shells give climbers a jacket that keeps out rain and lets out sweat.
Techwear labels build black city shells from membrane laminates with taped seams.
Gorpcore wears the bright membrane shell of the trail in the city.

origin.note: Michel Bras built a vegetable dish of dozens of wild and garden plants, the gargouillou, from the plateau around his restaurant.

adoptions.via: René Redzepi and the forager Roland Rittman took wild plants into the daily menu of Noma.

origin.note: Health Goth group posts share 3D renders of blade and mesh forms with no people.

adoptions.via: Health Goth posts show black 3D forms next to sport labels.

origin.note: Adobe Illustrator 8 adds the gradient mesh tool.

adoptions.via: Product sites blur large colour blobs into soft aurora fields behind the hero.
Hyperpop covers use soft pastel mesh gradients as the ground for chrome objects and stickers.
Ethereal pages fade pale pastel fields into each other behind thin type.

origin.note: The steel eyelet appears, and the lacing of a corset can take a much stronger pull.

adoptions.via: Corset makers set steel eyelets at the back, and a tight lace gave the narrow waist of the hourglass.
The long, straight corset used rows of steel eyelets, and a maker could lace it to a fixed line.

origin.note: Ludwig von Siegen makes a portrait of Amalia Elisabeth, Landgravine of Hesse-Kassel in the new tone process.

adoptions.via: London engravers such as John Raphael Smith and Valentine Green reproduce the portraits of Reynolds and Gainsborough, and Europe calls it the English manner.

origin.note: The state workshops of the First Emperor make heads and hands in moulds and join them to hand-built bodies.

adoptions.via: Workshops build the torso by coils, press the head in a two-piece mould and finish each face by hand.
Meissen modellers cast figures in many small piece moulds and join arms, heads and props with slip.
Vincennes and Sèvres cast biscuit figures in piece moulds, and cut the seams until they disappear.

origin.note: Josef Mueller-Brockmann and the journal Neue Grafik (1958) spread the modular grid for posters and print.

adoptions.via: Dieter Rams builds the 606 shelving system on a grid of rails that a user extends at will.
Otl Aicher builds the corporate design of Lufthansa on a fixed grid of marks, type and colour.
Unimark issues the New York City Transit Graphics Standards Manual, with sign grids for the whole system.
Windows Phone 7 builds its start screen from square and wide live tiles on one grid.
Bootstrap 2.0 ships a 12 column fluid grid for web pages.
Interfaces that follow the Braun products of Dieter Rams put each control in one cell of a strict grid.

origin.note: Carême set the grand sauces (espagnole, velouté, allemande and béchamel) as the base of his sauce chapters.

adoptions.via: Escoffier cut the grand sauces to five mother sauces in Le Guide culinaire.

origin.note: Jamie Beck and Kevin Burg publish the first cinemagraphs and use the name.

adoptions.via: The pair shows cinemagraphs of fashion week on Tumblr; brands and photographers copy the form.

origin.note: Disney's multiplane camera moves painted glass layers at different speeds; The Old Mill (1937) is its first film.

adoptions.via: Moon Patrol scrolls 3 background layers at different speeds in arcades.
16-bit consoles scroll 2 to 4 hardware layers for parallax depth.
Parallax scroll pages move the background layers slower than the page.
Layered app icons on tvOS, and later visionOS, tilt their layers with parallax.

origin.note: Van Cleef and Arpels patent the mystery setting, with stones of one colour on a hidden rail.

adoptions.via: Paris houses set rubies and sapphires so that no metal shows between the stones in flat Art Deco clips.
Small mystery-set rubies make the spray of colour at the centre of a gold bow.

origin.note: Georges Claude shows his neon tube at the Paris Motor Show in 1910, and a Paris hairdresser installs a neon sign in 1912.

adoptions.via: Venturi, Scott Brown and Izenour study the neon signs of the Las Vegas Strip in Learning from Las Vegas.
Ridley Scott fills the wet night streets of Blade Runner with neon signs.
Web designers fake neon with layered text-shadow and box-shadow glows once browsers support CSS3.

origin.note: Theo van Doesburg starts the magazine De Stijl; Piet Mondrian publishes his ideas on the new plastic in painting there.

adoptions.via: Gerrit Rietveld builds the Schröder House in Utrecht from planes and bars in white, grey and primary colours.
Web pages split the screen with black rules into white and primary-colour fields.

origin.note: Georges Seurat shows A Sunday on La Grande Jatte at the last Impressionist exhibition.

adoptions.via: The Autochrome plate of the Lumière brothers builds colour from dyed starch grains, and pictorialists use it for soft colour pictures.

origin.note: The LINE messenger launches with drawn sticker packs that users buy and send.

adoptions.via: LINE sticker packs spread the form across Asia, and other messengers copy it.

origin.note: Jingdezhen potters add the first on-glaze enamel colours to blue-and-white porcelain.

adoptions.via: Arita potters of the Kakiemon workshop fix a clear red and soft green on a milk-white body.
Kyoto potters paint enamel and gold on a pale crackle glaze, as Ninsei did at the Omuro kiln.
Johann Gregorius Höroldt arrives at Meissen and builds a palette of enamel colours for the hard-paste porcelain.
English porcelain factories paint flowers and insects in enamel on soft-paste tea ware.
Painters of the State Porcelain Factory fix flat planes of black and red enamel on white cups.

origin.note: Gadget fans film the opening of a new device from above and post the clip, and the plain framing becomes the norm of the unboxing video.

adoptions.via: Gadget fans post top-down clips of new devices on video sites.
Close-mic channels use the same fixed top-down frame for tapping and sorting objects.

origin.note: Ottoman marbled paper appears in the margins of a Hâlnâma manuscript of 1539–40. Older Persian or Central Asian sheets are possible.

adoptions.via: Ottoman scribes and binders use marbled paper in the margins and the covers of manuscripts, and the craft grows into the art of ebru.

origin.note: Parametric CAD comes from engineering (Sketchpad 1963, Pro/ENGINEER 1988); the office of Frank Gehry first uses CATIA in architecture to model and build the Fish in Barcelona.

adoptions.via: Patrik Schumacher names Parametricism at the Venice Architecture Biennale; Zaha Hadid Architects scripts whole facades.

origin.note: Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrates linear perspective; Alberti writes the method down in De pictura (1435).

adoptions.via: Stanley Kubrick sets corridors and rooms on one central vanishing point in 2001: A Space Odyssey; Wes Anderson later builds whole films on the flat, centred frame.
Cassette Futurism screens and sleeves draw wireframe floors to a horizon.
Tron draws vector grids that run to a horizon.
Vaporwave draws neon grid floors under a sunset.

origin.note: The Hipstamatic phone app applies lens and film looks to a photo with one tap.

adoptions.via: Instagram adds named filters such as Valencia and X-Pro II to square phone photos.
VSCO sells film-stock presets with short codes such as A6.
Profile owners apply one preset to every photo so that the grid has one tone.

origin.note: Xerox sells the 914, the first automatic plain-paper office copier.

adoptions.via: Mark Perry copies the paste-ups of Sniffin' Glue on an office copier, and punk zines follow.

origin.note: Henry Fox Talbot patented his photographic engraving in 1852.

adoptions.via: Karel Klíč makes the mature Talbot-Klič process, which stays in use.
Alfred Stieglitz prints the plates of Camera Work as photogravures.

origin.note: Raoul Hausmann and Hannah Höch of Berlin Dada cut press photographs and paste them into one sheet.

adoptions.via: Alexander Rodchenko and El Lissitzky use photomontage in Constructivist posters and books.
Klucis and Rodchenko paste cut photographs and drawn shapes into posters, covers and book jackets in Moscow.
Sergei Eisenstein carries the collision of fragments into the cut of Strike and Battleship Potemkin.
Superstudio sets mirrored grids into photographs of landscapes in the Continuous Monument.
Punk zines and record sleeves cut up newspapers with scissors and glue.
Photoshop makes the cut and the layer digital; early cyberculture prints dense photo-illustration.
Seapunk artists cut 1990s 3D shapes, dolphins and water textures into one collage on a turquoise ground.
Designers cut photographs of objects and clouds into collage scenes, in the line of the Surrealist collages of Max Ernst.
Anti-design sites overlap cut images and text blocks across a broken grid.
Scrapbook interfaces lay cut photographs, tape and stickers over each other, as on the page of an album.

origin.note: The Lumitype, also called Photon, of René Higonnet and Louis Moyroud sets type from a film disc with light.

adoptions.via: Adrian Frutiger draws Univers as one system of 21 weights and widths, for the Lumitype and for metal.

origin.note: Brent Burley presents the Disney principled BRDF at SIGGRAPH.

adoptions.via: Brian Karis presents the Unreal Engine 4 shading model at SIGGRAPH; engines move to metal-roughness materials.

origin.note: Game players add a webcam window to their capture of the screen, so that their reaction shows next to the game.

adoptions.via: Players overlay a webcam window on screen captures of games.
Live stream layouts keep the face window as a fixed slot.

origin.note: Ken Knowlton writes BEFLIX, a language that draws computer films as grids of cells in a small set of grey tones.

adoptions.via: The Xerox Alto has a bitmap display, and its programs draw icons cell by cell.
The Famicom builds every screen from 8×8 tiles in a fixed palette.
Susan Kare draws the Macintosh icons and the Chicago bitmap face on a grid of 32 by 32 cells.
Knight Lore draws isometric rooms cell by cell on the ZX Spectrum.
Zuzana Licko draws the Emigre bitmap faces for the 72 dpi screen and the dot-matrix printer.
The Game Boy limits the grid to 160×144 cells in four shades.
The Super Famicom widens the palette to 256 colours on screen.
The eBoy group publishes pixel illustrations of cities and objects on the web.
Japanese portal pages set text at 10 to 12 px in bitmap kanji fonts, so each glyph sits on the pixel grid.
Shigetaka Kurita draws the 176 emoji of the i-mode phone on a 12 by 12 pixel grid.

origin.note: Salvatore Ferragamo makes wedge soles of cork when leather is scarce.

adoptions.via: Glam rock musicians and makers raise the platform to 10 cm and cover it in bright colours.

origin.note: Paris jewellers mount diamonds in platinum, which is stronger than silver and does not tarnish.

adoptions.via: Cartier and other Paris houses make lace-like garlands and tiaras in platinum and diamond.
Platinum frames hold baguette diamonds and onyx in hard, flat geometric jewels.

origin.note: Painters such as Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes make small oil sketches outdoors; the collapsible paint tube (John Goffe Rand, 1841) later makes the work practical.

adoptions.via: The Skagen painters and other Nordic painters work on the beach and in the summer night light.
Rome Open City is shot on real streets in daylight, with little added light.
Cottagecore images of picnics, fields and gardens in open daylight echo the painters who worked outdoors.

origin.note: Kisho Kurokawa completes the Nakagin Capsule Tower with 140 steel cells on two concrete cores.

adoptions.via: Kisho Kurokawa bolts 140 prefabricated capsules to two concrete cores at the Nakagin Capsule Tower.

origin.note: Paul Iribe's album Les Robes de Paul Poiret is coloured by hand through stencils, and Paris fashion takes up the method. This is a landmark, not the first use: André Marty and Jean Saudé ran stencil studios in the 1890s.

adoptions.via: Lucien Vogel launches the Gazette du Bon Ton, with plates by Barbier, Lepape and Martin coloured in pochoir.
Artists of ROSTA paint news strips through paper stencils, one stencil for each colour, for the shop windows of Moscow.

origin.note: George Bickham's The Universal Penman engraves the roundhand of the English writing masters, the model for every later formal script.

adoptions.via: Engraved copybooks of the writing masters, then metal scripts that copy the plates.
Frank Mason Robinson writes the Coca-Cola wordmark in Spencerian, a pointed-pen hand.

origin.note: Malden Mills makes a napped polyester knit with Patagonia.

adoptions.via: Polartec fleece goes under the hard shell as the mid layer of the alpine kit.
Gorpcore wears the fleece jacket in the city as a bright outer layer.

origin.note: Digg, launched in 2004, lets its users vote links up (digging) or down (burying). This record dates the technique from Digg.

adoptions.via: Reddit adds up and down votes on each post and on each comment.

origin.note: Fresco painters transfer cartoons to wet plaster with pounced dots (spolvero).

adoptions.via: Delft tile painters pounce one pattern onto many tiles with a pricked sheet, the spons.
Delft painters pounce the same pattern onto many plates and tiles with a pricked sheet, the spons.

origin.note: Cyan's Myst shows its island as a set of pre-rendered still views.

adoptions.via: Resident Evil sets polygon figures over pre-rendered rooms on the PlayStation.

adoptions.via: The workshops of Arretium press stamped bowls in fired moulds and coat them with a red slip.

origin.note: Kazimir Malevich shows the Black Square and other pure shapes at the 0,10 exhibition.

adoptions.via: Wassily Kandinsky asks Bauhaus students to match the circle, the square and the triangle to blue, red and yellow.
Malevich and his pupils build a teapot and cups from blocks and cylinders at the State Porcelain Factory.
Designers at the Berlin and Halle porcelain works build services from the circle, the cylinder and the flat disc.
Yusaku Kamekura puts one red circle over gold type on the poster for the Tokyo 1964 Olympic Games.
Memphis Milano sets circles, triangles and squiggles on furniture and prints in loud colour.

origin.note: Myspace allowed users to add their own HTML and CSS to a profile.

adoptions.via: Myspace members restyle their profile pages with pasted code.

origin.note: Waldo Semon makes plasticised PVC at the B.F. Goodrich laboratory.

adoptions.via: Mary Quant shows the Wet collection of shiny PVC raincoats in bright colours.

origin.note: The Zsolnay factory develops pyrogranite, a frost-proof body for architectural ceramics.

adoptions.via: Ödön Lechner and the Zsolnay factory use pyrogranite tile and relief for the roofs and facades of Budapest.

origin.note: Warren Marrison builds the first quartz clock at Bell Telephone Laboratories.

adoptions.via: The Astron puts a quartz crystal in a wristwatch, and the quartz watch with digits follows.
The Swatch uses a quartz module of few parts, so that the watch is cheap and exact.

origin.note: Iznik potters add a raised red to the palette from about 1560, after the first use on lamps for Süleyman.

adoptions.via: Iznik potters paint tulips and carnations in raised red on tiles for the mosques of Istanbul.

origin.note: Chōjirō fires hand-built bowls one at a time for Sen no Rikyū and pulls them from the hot kiln.

adoptions.via: The Raku workshop fires each tea bowl alone and pulls it hot from the kiln.

origin.note: Wilhelm Barfuss improves the warp-knitting frame and creates the Raschel machine.

adoptions.via: The Raschel machine proved the most adaptable to nylon in the 1950s, and it knitted the mesh of girdles.
Warp-knit nylon gave the sheer, light stretch of the soft bra and the bodysuit.
Warp-knit elastane mesh gave the smooth control panel of the footless tights.

origin.note: Potters at the Yue kilns fire green-glazed stoneware in a kiln with a smoky, low-air flame.

adoptions.via: Bernard Leach builds a Japanese climbing kiln at St Ives and fires ash and celadon glazes in reduction at 1280 °C.

origin.note: Fernand Point built the menu of La Pyramide on Bresse poultry, crayfish, cream and Rhône wine.

adoptions.via: Pupils of Point, among them Bocuse and the Troisgros brothers, took the market menu into nouvelle cuisine.

origin.note: Riso Kagaku sells the first machine under the Risograph name, for schools, churches and offices.

adoptions.via: Art and zine studios buy used duplicators and print books and posters in fluorescent spot inks.

origin.note: The inscription at the base of Trajan's Column sets the model for Roman capitals.

adoptions.via: Nicolas Jenson prints in Venice with a roman face whose capitals follow Roman inscriptions.
Edward Johnston draws the London Underground block letters on the proportions of Roman capitals.
Hermann Zapf releases Optima, a sans serif whose shapes come from stone inscriptions he saw in Florence.

origin.note: The dome of the Pantheon has an open oculus 8.9 m wide; it is the only source of light.

adoptions.via: Alvar Aalto cuts many round, deep roof lights into the reading room of the Viipuri Library.

origin.note: La Varenne printed the roux as a sauce base in place of bread crumbs, and the stock as the base of a sauce and a soup.

adoptions.via: Carême built his grand sauces on stocks and a roux.
Escoffier kept the roux and the stock in the system of the hotel kitchen.
The restaurants of the provinces kept the classic stock and roux sauces.

origin.note: Charles Goodyear finds that rubber heated with sulphur stays elastic.

adoptions.via: The canvas basketball shoe has a vulcanised rubber sole that grips the court.

origin.note: Saddlers sew by hand with two needles; Thierry Hermès opens a harness workshop in Paris in 1837, and the stitch passes later into fine leather goods.

adoptions.via: The Kelly bag, a structured box bag, is stitched by hand in the saddler's way.
Houses of unmarked leather goods show the hand stitch as the only mark on the outside.

origin.note: Potters of Siegburg and Raeren glaze stoneware with salt in the 15th century.

adoptions.via: Rhineland potters glaze jugs and jars with salt from about 1400, so that the pots hold liquids without a lead lining.
American potters throw salt in the kiln to glaze crocks and jugs, with the same method that the Rhenish potters use.

origin.note: Goryeo potters inlay celadon with white and black slip.

adoptions.via: Goryeo potters inlay cranes, clouds and flowers in the green celadon.
Early Joseon potters use the same inlay on grey stoneware under a white slip.

origin.note: Users share cropped captures of posts outside their site, as proof of what a person wrote.

adoptions.via: Humour accounts turn the post screenshot into a main joke form.

origin.note: Samuel Simon patents the use of silk as a screen for stencil printing; sign and textile printers take it up.

adoptions.via: Andy Warhol starts to make photographic silkscreens in his studio and prints portraits in flat, loud colour.
Warhol and Rauschenberg pull photo screens onto painted canvas.
Poster studios screen print posters in flat, bright colours for clubs and protests.
The King's Road shop screen prints slogans and images on plain cotton T-shirts for the London punk scene.
Surf and skate labels screen print a name or a mark on the chest of a plain T-shirt and sell it in small runs.
Memphis designers put bold stripes, dots and speckles on ceramic vessels by screen print and decal, and fire the pattern on the glaze.
The Lima artist Monky begins to screen print his chicha posters with Juan Tenicela.
Dapper Dan prints luxury logos on leather with a silk-screen press and makes jackets and bags of it.

origin.note: A case maker patents the Oyster case with a screw-down crown; Rolex sells the watch under the name Oyster.

adoptions.via: The diver watch uses a screw-down crown and a screw-down case back to seal the case to 100 m.

origin.note: Claude Monet shows a group of Haystacks canvases, each of one motif in a different light.

adoptions.via: Karl Blossfeldt's book Urformen der Kunst shows plant forms one by one in a uniform series.
Kaj Franck repeats a few plain shapes as a modular set, so that the buyer builds a service from parts.
Frank Stella starts his Black Paintings, in which equal stripes repeat the shape of the canvas.
Bernd and Hilla Becher begin their typologies of water towers, blast furnaces and houses on one fixed frame.
Andy Warhol repeats one soup can or one face in a grid of identical canvases.

origin.note: Medieval feasts put many dishes on the table at once, in two or three services.

adoptions.via: Scappi and the banquet cooks of Italy planned each service as a pattern of dishes.
La Varenne wrote his book for a table of services of dishes in a fixed order.
Carême drew table plans for each service and published them.

origin.note: Carlo Scarpa separates new steel and stone from the old walls with narrow joints in the Castelvecchio museum (1957 to 1964).

adoptions.via: Carlo Scarpa finishes the Castelvecchio in Verona; each new element touches the old fabric along a visible gap.
John Pawson and Claudio Silvestrin set plaster and doors flush, with recessed joints in place of trim.
Peter Zumthor and other critical regionalists use the shadow line between materials as their detail.
Super Normal products set a narrow recessed gap between the parts of a plain body.

origin.note: Budd makes the first all-steel car body in a press for Dodge.

adoptions.via: Large presses form the wings and the roof of a streamlined body in single panels.
Presses form deep panels, and the fin is a pressed shape welded to the rear wing.
Presses make the long bonnet and the short deck of the Mustang in large numbers.
Deep draws give the round, joined body of the small one-box car.

origin.where: Paris, France, and Hollywood, United States
origin.note: Elsa Schiaparelli and Hollywood costume designers build wide padded shoulders into women's jackets in the 1930s.

adoptions.via: Armani and the houses of Milan and New York cut the padded shoulder into the working woman's suit.

origin.note: Greek vase painters fill figures with black slip and scratch the detail.

adoptions.via: Cut black paper profiles become a fashion in France and take the name of the minister Etienne de Silhouette.
Lotte Reiniger shows The Adventures of Prince Achmed, a feature film of cut paper silhouettes.
Otl Aicher draws the Munich Olympic pictograms as white-on-colour figure silhouettes.
Font Awesome 1.0 gives the web a free set of solid glyphs in an icon font.

origin.note: Robert Delaunay builds his Windows pictures from contrasts of pure colour, after the law of Michel-Eugène Chevreul (1839).

adoptions.via: Sonia Delaunay shows simultaneous fabrics and clothes of colour blocks at the Boutique Simultanée in Paris.

origin.note: Set photos of a Barbie film show cars, houses and clothes in one pink.

adoptions.via: Photographs and shop pages from the 2022 Barbie film set dress one pink across clothes, cars and houses.

origin.note: Ferran Adrià took the cream siphon of the pastry kitchen to make savoury foams at elBulli.

adoptions.via: Modernist Cuisine gave tested foam recipes, and modernist kitchens used the siphon for sauces and soups.

origin.note: Balsamiq Mockups draws wireframes with hand-drawn lines and a comic font, so that they look unfinished.

adoptions.via: Rage comics draw crude faces and stick bodies with a mouse in a basic paint program.
Wojak drawings use uneven mouse lines and flat fills.
Excalidraw and the Rough.js library draw diagrams and interface shapes with a jittered double stroke.

origin.note: Doric stone temples carve triglyphs and guttae that copy the beam ends and pegs of earlier timber temples.

adoptions.via: Mac OS X icons draw each application as a real object, such as a stamp, a clock or a disc.
iPhone OS copies notepads, leather, felt and brushed metal in its applications.

origin.note: Potters of Staffordshire start to cast earthenware in plaster moulds.

adoptions.via: Staffordshire potters cast and press earthenware figures in plaster moulds, so that one model gives many figures.
Parian makers cast figures from a thin slip in plaster moulds and fire them without a glaze.
Sanitary works cast WC pans, basins and cisterns in plaster moulds, so that one model gives many identical pieces.
Fireclay works cast the sink as one thick piece in a large plaster mould.
The works of T. G. Green casts jugs and teapots of Cornishware in plaster moulds and then bands them by hand.
Factories cast deco dancers and gazelles in plaster moulds, and paint each one by hand.
Works cast the basin, the pan and the bath of a set in plaster moulds and spray each with the same coloured glaze.

origin.note: Thomas Toft and other Staffordshire potters trail slip pictures on large dishes.

adoptions.via: Staffordshire potters trail cream slip pictures and names on red earthenware dishes.

origin.note: Leitz sells the Leica I, designed by Oskar Barnack.

adoptions.via: Henri Cartier-Bresson starts to photograph streets with a Leica.
Life magazine starts in 1936 and prints picture stories that photographers shoot with small, fast cameras.
Young photographers buy old 35 mm cameras and shoot colour negative and Tri-X film again.

origin.note: Helen Frankenthaler pours thinned oil on raw canvas in Mountains and Sea.

adoptions.via: Morris Louis and Kenneth Noland visit the studio of Frankenthaler and take up the stain method; Louis turns it into his Veils from 1954.
Noland moves from oil to thinned acrylic, which stains the cloth with no halo; Louis stains with thinned Magna acrylic from the first Veils in 1954.

origin.note: Georges Pralus cooked foie gras in a sealed bag for the Troisgros kitchen to lose less fat.

adoptions.via: Chefs of the avant-garde kitchen, such as Heston Blumenthal, took the water bath into the tasting menu.
The book Modernist Cuisine gave tables of time and temperature for each food.

origin.note: Industrial designers apply the bands of aerodynamic trains and cars to radios, toasters and refrigerators.

adoptions.via: Raymond Loewy and his peers put chrome bands on household appliances and pencil sharpeners.

origin.note: Zack Snyder uses ramps between slow and fast motion in the fights of 300.

adoptions.via: CapCut and similar editors give a curve tool, and editors cut clips to music with ramps.

origin.note: The elBulli kitchen made the alginate sphere a dish in 2003; the gel came from the food industry.

adoptions.via: The book Modernist Cuisine set out the recipes and the times, and Alinea served spheres on the tasting menu.

origin.note: Abel Gance uses a triple screen in Napoléon.

adoptions.via: TikTok adds Duet: the new clip plays beside an existing clip in one vertical frame.

origin.note: Potters sponge colour on cheap earthenware for export to North America.

adoptions.via: Scottish and Staffordshire potters dab colour with a cut sponge on cheap earthenware for the home and for export.

origin.note: Staffordshire potters press white clay reliefs into moulds and fix them to the body of salt-glazed stoneware.

adoptions.via: Wedgwood workers press fine white sprigs of classical figures onto the stained jasper body of urns and vases.

origin.note: The steel cage replaces the layered petticoat and cuts the weight of the skirt.

adoptions.via: Day dress and ball gown skirts of the Second Empire stand out on a cage of steel hoops.

origin.note: Disney animators exaggerate the volume of a ball and a face; Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston name it the first of twelve principles in 1981.

adoptions.via: John Lasseter applies it to computer animation in Luxo Jr. and in his SIGGRAPH paper of 1987.
Spring-damped animation in iOS 7 lets interface elements overshoot and settle.
3D motion design renders soft bodies that wobble, inflate and bounce.

origin.note: Coloured window glass is older; the choir that Abbot Suger consecrates at Saint-Denis starts the tall Gothic window of coloured light.

adoptions.via: Victorian houses put coloured glass in doors, stair windows and fanlights.
Louis Comfort Tiffany and Jacques Gruber make leaded opalescent glass for lamps, ceilings and screens.

origin.note: Shoemakers fit a steel rod in a thin heel.

adoptions.via: Vivier and the couture houses fit thin steel-cored heels to the court shoe.

origin.note: The messaging app LINE adds sticker sets, and the die-cut sticker becomes a screen object.

adoptions.via: Kidcore pages and images stack die-cut stickers with white borders over bright grounds.

origin.note: Giulio Campagnola made tone with dots of the burin in place of lines.

adoptions.via: Francesco Bartolozzi and William Wynne Ryland make stipple engravings in red and black for the London market.

adoptions.via: Iznik potters make dishes and tiles of a white quartz body under a clear alkaline glaze.

adoptions.via: Other chat assistants and search tools copy the streamed answer.

origin.note: Late medieval feasts put an edible figure of sugar or paste, a subtlety, on the table between the services.

adoptions.via: Venetian and Roman cooks and sugar workers made large sculptures for the banquets of cardinals and popes.
Carême published his designs for the pièce montée in Le Pâtissier pittoresque.

origin.note: Rays from a half disc appear on Art Deco facades, gates and lift doors around the Paris exposition of decorative arts in 1925.

Art Deco furniture, screens and mirrors take the ray motif inside.
Clarice Cliff paints rays and bands of flat colour on Bizarre ware.
Hollywood decorators hang sunburst mirrors and starburst lights in the homes and sets of film stars.

Space Age signs, packaging and posters use starbursts as a sign of the future.
Neo-deco rooms bring back the fan and the sunburst in brass and glass.

origin.note: Engineers at a US electric company make the first cap-and-pin porcelain disc for a string on high-voltage lines.

adoptions.via: Porcelain works make the glazed disc of the string, and the string replaces the rigid pin insulator on high-voltage lines.

origin.note: The T-strap becomes the standard dance shoe of the 1920s.

adoptions.via: The T-strap holds the foot in the Charleston and gives the Deco shoe its graphic line.

origin.note: Tambour work from India and China reaches European workrooms in the 18th century, and it grows fast on muslin.

adoptions.via: Dressmakers sew white tambour borders on muslin gowns and shawls.
Paris embroidery houses use the hook to sew glass beads on chiffon for the dress of the 1920s.

origin.note: Jian potters of the Song dynasty make dark bowls for whisked tea, with streaks and spots that the kiln forms.

adoptions.via: Jian kilns dip stoneware tea bowls in an iron glaze and fire them in reduction.

origin.note: Venetian workers set marble offcuts in lime and polish the floor of palaces: terrazzo alla veneziana.

adoptions.via: Poured terrazzo with brass strips paves Art Deco lobbies.
Poured terrazzo floors go into mid-century homes, schools and airports.
Memphis Milano prints speckled chip patterns on plastic laminates and fabrics.
Memphis Milano uses terrazzo for table tops and prints terrazzo chips on laminate.
Terrazzo moves from the floor to tables, tiles, lamps and small objects.

origin.note: Scott Fahlman proposes :-) and :-( on a Carnegie Mellon message board.

adoptions.via: Japanese net users post upright faces such as (^_^) on bulletin boards and develop the kaomoji form.

origin.note: On 2channel a reply bumps its thread up; a poster can choose sage to reply with no bump.

adoptions.via: 4chan bumps a thread on each reply and deletes the old threads at the bottom of the board.

origin.note: Usenet links each reply to its parent, and newsreaders show the replies as a tree.

adoptions.via: Reddit groups the comments on each post as a thread.

origin.note: In the 1920s Hollywood cameramen light stars with a key, a fill and a back light; in the 1930s the method is the studio standard.

adoptions.via: George Hurrell and other studio portraitists bring key, fill and back light to portraits for film and fashion magazines.
Creators light skin with a soft key at the window, a fill and a ring light, which gives the dewy sheen.

origin.note: Corinthian potters learn to make a black gloss and a red clay in one firing.

adoptions.via: Corinthian and Athenian painters draw black silhouettes in gloss slip, and the three stages fix the black.
Athenian painters keep the same firing and paint the background black instead of the figure.

origin.note: Hans Coper throws parts of a vessel on the wheel and joins them into stems, discs and spades.

adoptions.via: Hans Coper joins thrown cylinders, discs and bowls into bottles and cup forms in Lucie Rie's studio.

origin.note: Picasso asks the throwers at the Madoura pottery for plain forms and turns them into owls, bulls and women.

adoptions.via: Picasso alters thrown vases at the Madoura pottery, and the editions copy his altered forms.
Voulkos and his students cut and tear thrown cylinders, and stack them into large forms.

origin.note: A change in the ranking of the site to reward watch time makes the image that wins a click a main part of a video.

adoptions.via: Creators on YouTube compete for clicks with loud, face-led stills.
Short video makers copy the bold words and strong colour into caption frames.

origin.note: Cloth with tied resist patterns, known as shibori, survives from Japan of the eighth century.

adoptions.via: American counterculture makers dye T-shirts and skirts at home, and wear them at concerts and festivals.

origin.note: Netscape Navigator 1.1 added background images for pages.

adoptions.via: Free home page hosts make the tile a common ground for personal pages.
Profile owners set a wallpaper under their boxes with pasted CSS.

origin.note: A Council commission of 1767 leads to a new Swedish stove design with narrow flues and a closed damper.

adoptions.via: Swedish architects and potteries make tiled stoves with a closed damper for city flats and manors.

origin.note: Theodor Scheimpflug patents the rule for tilted lens and plane of focus.

adoptions.via: Paul Strand and Alfred Stieglitz use large view cameras for sharp, unretouched prints.
Group f/64 use large-format view cameras with small stops and sharp focus from front to back.
Julius Shulman photographs Case Study House No. 22 on a large-format camera with upright lines.
Nikon sells the PC-Nikkor 35mm f/3.5, the first shift lens for a 35mm camera.
Stephen Shore and Joel Sternfeld use 8 x 10 in view cameras with movements for large colour prints.
Food photographers tilt the plane of focus so that one bite is sharp and the rest falls away.
Interior photographers for Nordic magazines and blogs use shift lenses to keep walls vertical.
Photoshop CS6 adds the Tilt-Shift blur filter, and the miniature look spreads on the web.
Octopath Traveler blurs the top and bottom of each frame so the world reads as a miniature.

origin.note: Abbasid potters add tin oxide to lead glaze to copy white Chinese porcelain.

adoptions.via: Luca della Robbia covers terracotta sculpture with white tin glaze, so that church reliefs stand in the weather.
Italian potters paint cobalt labels on the white tin glaze of drug jars made for the shelves of pharmacies.
Urbino painters brush whole scenes on the raw tin glaze before the firing, so that the colours sink into the glaze.

origin.note: Charles Frederick Worth makes the fitted toile a standard step of the couture house.

adoptions.via: The House of Worth fits each cage-crinoline gown on a toile before it cuts the silk.
The Dior ateliers fit each New Look piece on a toile, so that the built waist and the full skirt fall right.
The ateliers of Hamburg and Milan fit a plain jacket on a toile again and again, to set a clean cut with no seam to spare.

origin.note: Abraham-Louis Breguet patents the tourbillon on 26 June 1801.

adoptions.via: Breguet fits the tourbillon to a pocket watch to cancel the error that gravity causes in the upright position.

origin.note: John Sadler and Guy Green of Liverpool print tiles and Worcester soon prints porcelain.

adoptions.via: Soft-paste tea ware takes printed landscapes and flower designs in black and blue.

origin.note: Andrea Mantegna paints an open oculus with figures that look down into the Camera degli Sposi (1465 to 1474).

adoptions.via: Giulio Romano paints the Sala dei Giganti in Mantua so that the walls and the vault seem to fall on the viewer.
Andrea Pozzo paints a false dome and an open vault over the nave of Sant'Ignazio in Rome.

origin.note: Mills of the Borders weave the woollen twill, and a London merchant reads the name 'tweel' as 'tweed'.

adoptions.via: Highland estates order district checks in tweed for the keeper and the guest, and tailors cut sporting jackets from them.

origin.note: English potters print cobalt blue patterns under the glaze from engraved plates.

adoptions.via: Staffordshire potters print the willow pattern in blue on cheap earthenware plates from one copper plate.

origin.note: Normcore feeds and posts show ordinary clothes in plain snapshots.

adoptions.via: Normcore catalogues and feeds show clothes and people in flat daylight, front-on, with no filter and no props.

origin.note: Homer Laughlin makes the red of Fiesta ware with uranium oxide.

adoptions.via: Frederick Rhead and Homer Laughlin fire the red Fiesta glaze with uranium oxide.

origin.note: Spacewar! runs on the point-plotting display of the PDP-1.

adoptions.via: Atari ships Asteroids and Lunar Lander on vector monitors in arcades.

origin.note: FutureSplash Animator added vector tweens for the web; Macromedia later renamed it Flash.

adoptions.via: Agencies build full sites as Flash timelines with intros and animated menus.

origin.note: Factories coat sheet iron and cast iron with glass powder, and the process makes cheap, washable pots, signs and baths.

adoptions.via: Craft jewellers fuse coloured glass to silver and copper in small, hand-made jewels.
Jewellers fuse translucent enamel on gold in the Art Nouveau jewel, at times with no metal backing.
Factories and workshops fit enamelled steel shades, signs and fittings that are hard, bright and easy to wash.
Jewellers fire enamel on guilloché metal for vanity cases and evening bags in the Art Deco style.

origin.note: Comanche draws its terrain with the Voxel Space engine.

adoptions.via: Infiniminer and Minecraft build whole worlds from cube cells.

origin.note: Bill Bowerman pours rubber into his wife's waffle iron to make a light, grippy sole.

adoptions.via: The waffle racing flat is the first running shoe that grips a track and a road in the same way.

origin.note: Toto launches the Washlet, a toilet seat with a warm-water spray, for the Japanese home.

adoptions.via: A Japanese maker fits the seat on a plain vitreous china WC, and the seat carries the water, heat and control.
Designer ranges adopt the seat on a wall-hung bowl as an option.

origin.note: Sailors and fishermen soak canvas in linseed oil to make it shed water.

adoptions.via: Scottish makers dress cotton with paraffin wax, which does not stiffen in the cold, for the country jacket.
A Swedish maker of outdoor kit waxes poly-cotton twill for the Nordic field jacket.

origin.note: Auguste de Méritens joins lead plates with a carbon arc; oxy-acetylene gas welding follows in 1903.

adoptions.via: Car bodies change from wood frames to all-steel welded shells and roofs.
Welded steel rod makes light bases and frames for chairs and tables.
High-frequency welding joins the seams of PVC and vinyl clothes.
Jewellers leave the weld and the hammer mark in view on silver and gold.
Loft furniture shows its welds and bolts as a sign of the factory.
Ultrasonic welding seals the quartz module into the plastic watch case.

origin.note: Victor Horta uses curved iron stems on the stair and the ceiling of the Hotel Tassel.

adoptions.via: Victor Horta carries the iron whiplash line into the stair, the floor mosaic and the wall paint of the Hotel Tassel in Brussels.
Hermann Obrist shows the Cyclamen wall hanging, an embroidery of one long curved stem.
Tile makers press the S-curve of the plant stem in low relief on hearth tiles and friezes.
Jugend and Pan magazines print initials and vignettes in interlaced curved lines.
Hector Guimard casts the whiplash line into the railings, handles and stoves of the Castel Béranger.
Otto Eckmann draws the Eckmann-Schrift with brush-like curved strokes.
Hector Guimard designs the iron entrances of the Paris Metro with plant-like curves.
Rozenburg of The Hague shows eggshell porcelain with whiplash curves at the Exposition Universelle in Paris, and French potters show flambé vases with plant forms.
San Francisco concert posters of 1966 to 1968 copy Art Nouveau lettering and whiplash curves.

origin.note: Francis Wenham builds the first wind tunnel for the Aeronautical Society.

adoptions.via: Designers test streamlined bodies in the tunnel and cut the drag.
Designers tune the smooth underbody and the small mirrors in the tunnel.
Makers tune the flat floor and the flush door handles for range.

origin.note: Hong Kong films hang actors on wires before the 1980s; Zu Warriors from the Magic Mountain (1983) is a landmark of the special-effects wuxia film, not the first use.

adoptions.via: Yuen Woo-ping choreographs the wire fights of The Matrix for Hollywood.

origin.note: Thomas Bewick developed the technique at the end of the 18th century.

adoptions.via: Thomas Bewick publishes the first volume of A History of British Birds, with wood engravings in the text.
The Dalziel Brothers start a London firm that cuts blocks for the illustrated press.

origin.note: Darius Wells makes wood type in quantity with a routing machine, and the poster printers take it up at once.

adoptions.via: The first wood type lines are fat faces copied from the London founders.
Wood type founders add Egyptian slabs and condensed letters for posters.
Trade cards and shop signs set the name of the firm in heavy wood letters.
Hatch Show Print opens in Nashville and prints show bills from wood type and cuts for circuses, minstrels and later country music.

origin.note: The Diamond Sutra, printed in China in 868, is the oldest dated printed book made from woodblocks.

adoptions.via: Michael Wolgemut and Wilhelm Pleydenwurff design the 1,809 woodcuts of the Nuremberg Chronicle, which Anton Koberger prints with the text.
Lucas Cranach the Elder and Hans Burgkmair print woodcuts from a line block and tone blocks; Ugo da Carpi follows in Italy.
Workshops in Dong Ho and Yangliuqing print an outline block and flat colour blocks for New Year pictures.
Hu Zhengyan's Ten Bamboo Studio in Nanjing publishes its Manual of Painting and Calligraphy. The studio fits many small pearwood blocks into one picture and presses dry blocks for raised lines.
Print shops in Moscow and Kyiv cut cheap picture sheets on wood, and hand colourists paint them for sale by pedlars.
Suzuki Harunobu and his printers make the full-colour nishiki-e print on many blocks.
Suzuki Harunobu and his printers make the full-colour nishiki-e print in Edo, with one block for each colour and a kento register.
Poetry clubs in Edo pay for surimono, small prints on thick paper with embossing and metal dust.
The oldest invitation to a senjafuda exchange meeting that survives is from 1799. The slips are printed from woodblocks.
Bengali craftsmen cut woodblock pictures for books and sheets printed in the Battala quarter of Calcutta.
Meiji printers use imported aniline dye on woodblocks, and Kobayashi Kiyochika adds light and shadow in his kosen-ga.
William Morris draws woodcut borders and initials for the Kelmscott Press, cut by William Harcourt Hooper and others.
Paul Gauguin cuts the woodcuts of the Noa Noa series with flat colour and rough cuts.
Cutters in the Brazilian northeast cut woodblock covers for cordel chapbooks, from about 1900.
Yamamoto Kanae cuts and prints his own block for the print Fisherman, and so starts the sosaku-hanga movement.
Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Erich Heckel and Karl Schmidt-Rottluff of Die Brücke cut jagged woodcuts in Dresden.
Die Brücke artists cut rough woodcuts in Dresden, with flat shapes and visible gouge marks.
André Derain and Maurice de Vlaminck cut woodcuts with flat colour and rough gouge marks.
Watanabe Shozaburo restarts the three-trade woodblock shop in Tokyo and names its prints shin-hanga.
Lu Xun leads a woodcut class in Shanghai, and young artists cut black-and-white prints on cheap wood.

origin.note: Short video apps add auto captions, and makers restyle them as large animated words that follow the speech.

adoptions.via: Short video apps and editing tools add auto captions that makers restyle as animated words.

origin.note: Arthur Kneibler designs a short brief with an overlapping Y-shaped fly.

adoptions.via: Coopers, Inc. launched the Y-front brief in a store in Chicago on 19 January 1935.

origin.note: Thomas Burberry makes gabardine from proofed yarn.

adoptions.via: Burberry cuts the gabardine into the officer's trench coat for the War Office.
Burberry supplies windproof gabardine smocks to the Everest party.

origin.note: Yixing potters build small unglazed teapots by hand, as steeped tea replaces whisked tea.

adoptions.via: Yixing potters build every pot by hand from slabs and strips, and stamp it with a seal.
